screenings.title: Galaxie
screenings.description: A pinnacle of the art of filmic portraiture, Gregory Markopoulos’s GALAXIE comprises thirty short portraits of men and women from across the spectrum of the mid-1960s cultural scene in New York City. Its subjects include many of Markopoulos’s fellow experimental filmmakers – Storm De Hirsch, George & Mike Kuchar, Jonas Mekas, Shirley Clarke, Amy Taubin, and Ed Emshwiller – as well as figures from the literary and art worlds, including Parker Tyler, Jasper Johns, W.H. Auden, Allen Ginsberg, Kenneth Kelman, Maurice Sendak, Susan Sontag, and others. In keeping with Markopoulos’s short-form masterpieces MING GREEN, BLISS, and SORROWS, each of the individual portraits in GALAXIE was edited entirely in-camera, a near-miraculous feat given the intricate use of multiple layers of superimposition, all of it achieved by rewinding and making additional passes through the single 100-foot (ca. 3-minute) roll of 16mm film during the shoot. Initially intending to produce only a handful of portraits, Markopoulos ended up filming 40 different chapters, and ultimately incorporated the first 30 into the completed work (presented in the order they were created). Each of the portraits represents an exquisite visual record of the encounter between subject and filmmaker, while the film as a whole provides an extraordinary opportunity to observe the gradual development of Markopoulos’s approach to portraiture and in-camera editing.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

When her own daughter’s future becomes entangled with the past, Vénéranda is forced to find her own words at last.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: Rate It X
screenings.description: First released in 1985, RATE IT X stunned audiences and critics alike with its unflinching look at how sexism and sexual exploitation are embedded in American media and culture. Directors Lucy Winer and Paula de Koenigsberg traveled across the United States interviewing men who profited from—and helped perpetuate—stereotyped and sexualized images of women. Advertising executives describe how sex is used to sell product. Hustler magazine’s creator of the notorious “Chester the Molester” cartoon proudly displays drawings depicting a predatory adult man entrapping young girls. A fundamentalist minister tells us that Adam shirked his responsibility by allowing Eve to lead. The flamboyant producer of a popular cable show roams the streets of New York City in a silver lamé jumpsuit, video camera in hand, asking young women, “Would you like to flex into a hallway and pose nude?”

screenings.title: Rome, Open City
screenings.description: “A STILL-THRILLING CALL TO CONSCIENCE AND HOPE! Shot with electrifying urgency months after Rome’s liberation… a cinematic landmark [that brought] Italian neorealism to world-wide attention. Born of wartime trauma and a desire for unity in the new Italy that would come, ROME, OPEN CITY has lost little of its power.” – Kristin M. Jones, Wall Street Journal Read the full review. “THE MOST PRECIOUS MOMENT OF FILM HISTORY!” – Martin Scorsese “ROSSELLINI’S NEOREALIST MASTERPIECE... Aldo Fabrizi is compelling as a sympathetic priest, as is Marcello Pagliero as a cool Communist. But towering over all is Anna Magnani, as a pregnant widow, mother and bride-to-be... Plain-spoken, tender and yet indomitable, she provides the film’s central anima.” – Andy Webster, New York Times “Rossellini’s tense, bloody, death-haunted film conjures an authenticity that’s based less on its quasi-documentary style than on a vision that brings ideas to life. It offers a template for a postwar renewal of Italy, as well as Italian cinema.” – Richard Brody, New Yorker “A LEGENDARY CINEMATIC ACHIEVEMENT! Its justly celebrated documentary aesthetic and naturalistic performances, aided by the filmmakers’ budgetary restrictions and the ruinous state of the postwar Italian film industry, help the work achieve moments of devastating, near miraculous beauty.” – Oleg Ivanov, Slant Read the full review. “The fame of Rossellini’s brutal, melodramatic account of the underground resistance to the Nazi occupation rest on its extraordinary immediacy and its rough, documentary look; at its most startling, it seems ‘caught’ rather than staged. Many Americans, used to slick war films, reacted to it as if it actually were caught… The movie gave us a cross-section of a city under terrible stress.” – Pauline Kael “Rossellini’s Neo-Realism masterpiece... It scarcely matters how many times you watch it... The story plays like a gripping thriller: a cat-and-mouse game between Gestapo and resistance cell.” – Cath Clarke, The Guardian “Still a picture of unrivaled immediacy and passion... memorably preserved a place and a time—and taught generations of filmmakers how to preserve theirs.” – Michael Wilmington “ALL ROADS LEAD TO ROME, OPEN CITY.” – Godard

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire

But times are changing for Harry. His daily pickpocket take isn’t green bills and wristwatches, it’s credit cards and cell phones. And one unfortunate night, cryptocurrency and a handgun. THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

When Caesar Was King
the Comedy Genius of Sid Caesar
screenings.description: In the early 1950s, 20 million people tuned into see the weekly TV extravaganza Your Show of Shows, starring Sid Caesar, a master of physical comedy, “double talk” and pantomime, supported by “second bananas” Imogene Coca, Carl Reiner, and Howard Morris, and a truly legendary writing staff that included Reiner, Lucille Kallen, Mel Tolkin, Mel Brooks, and Neil Simon (and, later, Woody Allen). This special compilation of some of Caesar’s greatest sketches, from Your Show of Shows and the later Caesar’s Hour, will be followed by an onstage conversation with Bruce Goldstein, Film Forum’s Founding Repertory Artistic Director (and Caesar fanatic), and longtime New York Times and Vanity Fair writer David Margolick, author of the definitive biography When Caesar Was King: How Sid Caesar Reinvented American Comedy (Schocken Books). Book signing in lobby following event. Produced and compiled by Bruce Goldstein. Edited by William Hohauser.

screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. screenings.title: Paisan
screenings.description: PAISÀ Italy, 1946 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Carmela Sazio, Robert Van Loon, Dots Johnson Approx. 126 min. 35mm. The story of Italy’s liberation, told in six episodes, traveling from the first Allied landing in Sicily to the battle of the Po Delta, PAISAN demonstrated that OPEN CITY had been no fluke. Conceived on a vaster scale, with a considerably higher budget, and international distribution from MGM, PAISAN is a national epic that still startles for its immediacy, its technical mastery, its unpredictable rhythms. Scenes of unbearable suspense on the streets of Florence alternate with lighter fare, such as the doctrinal scuffles between Italian monks and American chaplains in Romagna. Stitched together like a newsreel (and skillfully edited to blend in stock footage and suggest off-screen pyrotechnics with creative sound effects), PAISAN became a worldwide sensation, an intellectual action film that pictured recent history with an unprecedented heft and scope. The film became a lodestar for filmmakers from Gillo Pontecorvo to Martin Scorsese, with the latter remarking, “The result... is still startling: it’s like seeing reality itself unfolding before your eyes.” 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà.

screenings.title: Raise the Red Lantern
screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: Voyage to Italy
screenings.description: VIAGGIO IN ITALIA Italy/France, 1954 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman, George Sanders, Maria Mauban In Italian with English subtitles. Approx. 97 min. New 4K restoration. In Naples to sell a late uncle’s villa, London business man George Sanders and wife Ingrid Bergman find that, after eight years of marriage, they have little to say to each other. And as the closing drags on, Bergman remembers a died-too-young poet who loved her, Sanders frets about time away from work, and they split apart—she to stare at the rawness of the statuary in the Museum, the ionization of Vesuvian craters, the skeletons at the cemetery; he to dally with friends on Capri, languidly pursue an estranged wife, and to wave off an attractive prostitute; both to finally view the plaster molds of the dead of Pompeii. Little happens, and yet subtly we see the degeneration of a marriage. Will it take a miracle to save it? Unsuccessful on first release, but over the years steadily climbing the ranks of All-Time Ten Best lists. New 4K restoration from Cinecittà. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

As Indiana slowly eats one mushroom, the action is rendered mysterious by Warhol’s decision to assemble the rolls out of order, so the mushroom appears to magically renew itself from time to time.” –Callie Angell, MoMAAndy WarholBLOW JOB1964, 41 min, 16mm-to-DCP, silent. Collection of The Andy Warhol Museum, Pittsburgh; Contribution The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc.“Warhol’s unmoving camera remains focused in close-up on the head of a young man, never descending below his shoulders to show the sex act advertised by the film’s title, which is nevertheless legible, in slow motion, in the changing expressions passing across his face. By wittily restricting what his camera sees, Warhol frustrates the expectations of porn fans and film censors alike, while simultaneously implicating both audiences in the same illicit desire.” –Callie Angell, MoMATotal running time: ca. 75 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Harry is an old-school hustler. A classic native New Yorker, he moves through life lubricating palms with cash, relying on his wits and connections. But times are changing for Harry. His daily pickpocket take isn’t green bills and wristwatches, it’s credit cards and cell phones. And one unfortunate night, cryptocurrency and a handgun. THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

screenings.title: L'amore
screenings.description: Italy, 1948 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Anna Magnani, Federico Fellini, Peparuolo, Amelia Robert In Italian with English subtitles. Approx. 80 min. 35mm. Conceived as an homage to the range and artistry of Anna Magnani, L’AMORE is a diptych that drags the actress to the brink and watches, mouth agape, as she leaps into the abyss. The first part—“The Human Voice”—adapts a one-act play by Jean Cocteau, which Magnani had performed on stage in 1942, playing a woman whose only connection to her lover runs through the telephone wire. Shot in a French studio over two weeks with money that Rossellini had procured for GERMANY YEAR ZERO, this intensely claustrophobic showcase for Magnani (and her dog, Micia) renders a break-up as a world-historic event—as it always is for those so spurned. The second episode—“The Miracle”—was based on an original idea by Fellini, who also co-stars as a silent vagabond whom Magnani’s talkative goatherd believes to be the incarnation of Saint Joseph. Throwing herself upon the saint’s blissful body, Magnani wakes in a daze, pregnant and ever closer to the divine. If the monks can report sightings of the Madonna, why cannot Magnani follow her holy path? Although “The Miracle” aroused no complaints from the Vatican, it faced extraordinary hostility in the US, where the lay Catholics of the Legion of Decency launched a successful campaign for the New York Board of Regents to rescind the film’s exhibition license on the basis of alleged sacrilege. Distributor Joseph Burstyn appealed the decision all the way to the Supreme Court, which ultimately ruled in his favor, belatedly bringing cinema under the protection of the First Amendment, and sowing the seeds of censorship’s demise. A miracle indeed. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

screenings.title: Raise the Red Lantern
screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire

The second takes place in 2026 and stars Raúl, a screenwriter and director who is writing a script that we soon discover is the story of Elsa, her boyfriend Bonifacio, and her friends Patricia and Natalia. He looks inside himself, and he can't help but also look at the people who make up his most intimate universe: his partner and his assistant.

screenings.title: The Royal Ballet: the Nutcracker (2026)
screenings.description: At a cosy Christmas party, young Clara meets the mysterious magician Drosselmeyer, who gives her a nutcracker doll. When the guests have departed and the house is asleep, Clara sneaks downstairs in search of the doll. Instead, she finds Drosselmeyer, who whisks her away on a journey into a whole world of enchantment: fantastical landscapes of flurried snow and glittering confection where toys come alive and the magic never stops. Peter Wright’s production of this festive family favourite sparkles to the wondrous swell of Tchaikovsky’s orchestral score, alongside the glow and grandeur of Julia Trevelyan Oman’s period designs.

screenings.title: A Man Walks Down the Street
screenings.description: Raanan, a middle aged man, returns home after 30 years abroad. A chance encounter with an elderly man unlocks troubled memories, and a brief affair with a much younger man, send him spiraling through generational rifts, and force him to confront his internalized homophobia and emotional wounds of his past.

screenings.title: Rome, Open City
screenings.description: “A STILL-THRILLING CALL TO CONSCIENCE AND HOPE! Shot with electrifying urgency months after Rome’s liberation… a cinematic landmark [that brought] Italian neorealism to world-wide attention. Born of wartime trauma and a desire for unity in the new Italy that would come, ROME, OPEN CITY has lost little of its power.” – Kristin M. Jones, Wall Street Journal Read the full review. “THE MOST PRECIOUS MOMENT OF FILM HISTORY!” – Martin Scorsese “ROSSELLINI’S NEOREALIST MASTERPIECE... Aldo Fabrizi is compelling as a sympathetic priest, as is Marcello Pagliero as a cool Communist. But towering over all is Anna Magnani, as a pregnant widow, mother and bride-to-be... Plain-spoken, tender and yet indomitable, she provides the film’s central anima.” – Andy Webster, New York Times “Rossellini’s tense, bloody, death-haunted film conjures an authenticity that’s based less on its quasi-documentary style than on a vision that brings ideas to life. It offers a template for a postwar renewal of Italy, as well as Italian cinema.” – Richard Brody, New Yorker “A LEGENDARY CINEMATIC ACHIEVEMENT! Its justly celebrated documentary aesthetic and naturalistic performances, aided by the filmmakers’ budgetary restrictions and the ruinous state of the postwar Italian film industry, help the work achieve moments of devastating, near miraculous beauty.” – Oleg Ivanov, Slant Read the full review. “The fame of Rossellini’s brutal, melodramatic account of the underground resistance to the Nazi occupation rest on its extraordinary immediacy and its rough, documentary look; at its most startling, it seems ‘caught’ rather than staged. Many Americans, used to slick war films, reacted to it as if it actually were caught… The movie gave us a cross-section of a city under terrible stress.” – Pauline Kael “Rossellini’s Neo-Realism masterpiece... It scarcely matters how many times you watch it... The story plays like a gripping thriller: a cat-and-mouse game between Gestapo and resistance cell.” – Cath Clarke, The Guardian “Still a picture of unrivaled immediacy and passion... memorably preserved a place and a time—and taught generations of filmmakers how to preserve theirs.” – Michael Wilmington “ALL ROADS LEAD TO ROME, OPEN CITY.” – Godard

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: The Piano
screenings.description: Gale-force winds and interminable lashing rain render colonial New Zealand a nigh uninhabitable mire in Campion’s elemental Antipodean Gothic romance, in which mute Scotswoman Ada and her young daughter (Holly Hunter, Anna Paquin) arrive under the Southern Cross so that Ada can be wed to stiff-backed settler Alisdair Stewart (Sam Neill)—an arranged union that quickly sours when Stewart separates Ada from her lone means of expression, her piano, and Ada drifts into an increasingly compromising and sexualized relationship with neighbor George Baines (Harvey Keitel), an ex-sailor and the instrument’s new owner. With its Palme d’Or win at Cannes, Campion became the first female director to receive that honor—and a shower of Academy Awards still lay ahead.

screenings.title: Germany, Year Zero
screenings.description: GERMANIA, ANNO ZERO Italy/France/Germany, 1948 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Edmund Moeschke, Ernst Pittschau, Ingetraud Hinze Approx. 78 min. 35mm. Following the international acclaim and box office success of ROME, OPEN CITY and PAISAN, Rossellini took the first of many obstreperous swerves that would come to define his career. His next film would be another dispatch from war-torn Europe, with scenes playing out amidst the rubble with unvarnished immediacy, with unfamiliar and nonprofessional actors populating the cast—but this time, the protagonists would not be resistance fighters liberating Italy, but the defeated Germans muddling through their wasteland reich. Financed largely by the French government, GERMANY, YEAR ZERO became an experiment in radical empathy and its limits, casting about for signs of new life in a nation of crooks, unrepentant Nazis, and pederasts. The only innocent soul is twelve-year-old protagonist Edmund, who cannot qualify for a work permit, but must somehow earn a living to support his household. Even the child recognizes that he has no role models in this world: his brother is a mopey ex-soldier who refuses to register for a ration card, his father is an invalid who muses he’d be better off dead, his neighbors are coarse and severe, his friends are common swindlers, and his former school teacher still preaches that the strong must snuff out the weak. Unsentimental in the extreme and devoid of any comic relief, GERMANY YEAR ZERO plays like a seance for souls who have yet to recognize themselves as the walking dead. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà.

screenings.title: Minotaur
screenings.description: Intrigue, corruption, betrayal, survival: the walls of the maze are closing in. The latest from Oscar® nominated writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan), Cannes Grand Prix winner MINOTAUR is a twist-laden parable for our times. Russia, 2022. Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence. A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

Threading deep archival scholarship with today’s headlines, 14TH brings together legal minds, politicians, historians and cultural voices to explore a question America still hasn’t settled: Who gets to belong?

Through masterful cinematography often filmed in dangerous conditions – and the protagonist’s radiant energy – this empowering collaboration between an established filmmaker and a young new artist enables her to reclaim her identity. screenings.title: Stromboli
screenings.description: Italy/U.S., 1950 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Ingrid Bergman, Mario Vitale, Renzo Cesana, Mario Sponzo Approx. 106 min. 35mm. Upon seeing PAISAN in 1948, Ingrid Bergman sent Roberto Rossellini a fan letter, offering her services on any project he might want to make. “Well, who is this Ingrid Bergman?” asked Rossellini, unfamiliar with her work. Duly schooled and armed with a promissory note from Hollywood’s most popular actress, Rossellini went calling in California. After failing to come to terms with Samuel Goldwyn and David O. Selznick, Rossellini and Bergman signed a contract with Howard Hughes, the new owner of RKO Radio Pictures, who luckily had no need of reading a script beforehand. Bergman and Rossellini sailed for Stromboli, a remote island that would be the setting for their first picture together. Bergman plays Karin, a Lithuanian refugee whose only hope of getting out of a displaced persons camp after the war is to marry Antonio (Mario Vitale), a simple fisherman. Returning to his modest home on Stromboli, the couple faces one crisis after another: he is too poor to give her the life to which she’s accustomed, she is ostracized by the villagers for a lack of modesty. Nature asserts its supremacy, as volcanoes are wont to do. (Even Antonio’s “gift” of a pet ferret is a cruel reminder of the local food chain.) STROMBOLI becomes a vision quest, a groping towards cosmic grace that reveals a new vulnerability in Bergman that Hollywood never dared tap. Back on terra firma, Rossellini’s rangy artistry was quickly overshadowed by the revelation that he had begun an affair with Bergman and impregnated her. “Probably no film in history has received as much publicity as STROMBOLI,” noted Variety, but leering curiosity did not translate into ticket sales for this intuitively-constructed art film. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà.

screenings.title: Raise the Red Lantern
screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: The Cockpit
screenings.description: The “cockpit” of the title is a cramped apartment in the suburbs of Tokyo, unprepossessing in size but bursting with creative ferment, for this dinky flat is functioning as the recording studio where underground producer-rapper OMSB and cohort Bim are laying down a new track, to be titled “Curve Death Match.” Shot largely from a camera locked down to the workstation and facing the duo, The Cockpit follows the songwriting process from sampling to beat-making to writing to the final recording, in the process giving an intimate, pared-to-the-bone, nuts-and-bolts breakdown of the intricacies of hip-hop artistry without rival.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: The Flowers of St. Francis
screenings.description: FRANCESCO, GIULLARE DI DIO Italy, 1950 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Co-written by Federico Fellini Starring Aldo Fabrizi, Gianfranco Bellini, Peparuolo In Italian with English subtitles. Approx. 87 min. 35mm/4K restoration. Rossellini’s account of a brief period in the life of Saint Francis is as plainspoken and modest as its subject, an anti-hagiography closer to the mud below than the heavens above. Loosely inspired by Fioretti di San Francesco, a nearly-contemporaneous 14th-century collection of vignettes, the film was shaped into a bare ‘scenario’ by Rossellini and Federico Fellini, but the final result remains bracingly plotless. A series of parables that illustrate the moral quality of its characters rather than any scriptural interpretation, THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS is built from incidents and yarns: an encounter with a leper, a visit from Saint Clare, the quest for a pig’s foot, and the tale of the brother who keeps giving away his clothes. Francis is played by Brother Nazario Gerardi and the ranks of his disciples are populated by real-life monks that Rossellini featured in PAISAN; the only professional actor in sight is Aldo Fabrizi, with an extended cameo as a preening warlord. Financed by a credulous publisher who believed Rossellini would deliver a devout testament whose debut would coincide with the papally declared ‘Holy Year’ of 1950, THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS instead premiered in the aftermath of Rossellini’s unsaintly and adulterous dalliance with Ingrid Bergman. The initial critical reaction was indifferent, but Rossellini had the last laugh; in 1995, the Vatican named THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS among fifteen essential works of religious cinema. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà. 4K restoration courtesy Janus Films. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: L'amore
screenings.description: Italy, 1948 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Anna Magnani, Federico Fellini, Peparuolo, Amelia Robert In Italian with English subtitles. Approx. 80 min. 35mm. Conceived as an homage to the range and artistry of Anna Magnani, L’AMORE is a diptych that drags the actress to the brink and watches, mouth agape, as she leaps into the abyss. The first part—“The Human Voice”—adapts a one-act play by Jean Cocteau, which Magnani had performed on stage in 1942, playing a woman whose only connection to her lover runs through the telephone wire. Shot in a French studio over two weeks with money that Rossellini had procured for GERMANY YEAR ZERO, this intensely claustrophobic showcase for Magnani (and her dog, Micia) renders a break-up as a world-historic event—as it always is for those so spurned. The second episode—“The Miracle”—was based on an original idea by Fellini, who also co-stars as a silent vagabond whom Magnani’s talkative goatherd believes to be the incarnation of Saint Joseph. Throwing herself upon the saint’s blissful body, Magnani wakes in a daze, pregnant and ever closer to the divine. If the monks can report sightings of the Madonna, why cannot Magnani follow her holy path? Although “The Miracle” aroused no complaints from the Vatican, it faced extraordinary hostility in the US, where the lay Catholics of the Legion of Decency launched a successful campaign for the New York Board of Regents to rescind the film’s exhibition license on the basis of alleged sacrilege. Distributor Joseph Burstyn appealed the decision all the way to the Supreme Court, which ultimately ruled in his favor, belatedly bringing cinema under the protection of the First Amendment, and sowing the seeds of censorship’s demise. A miracle indeed. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

screenings.description: France/Italy, 1963 Directed by Jean-Luc Godard Co-written by Roberto Rossellini Starring Marino Masé, Patrice Moullet, Geneviève Galéa, Catherine Ribeiro, Barbet Schroeder Approx. 80 min. Jean-Luc Godard had long been a champion of Rossellini’s cinema (He famously stated, “All roads lead to Open City.”), even as the younger man’s own filmmaking quickly evolved towards a more modernist and abrasive style. (Upon seeing VIVRE SA VIE, Rossellini admonished Godard that his work was drifting towards “Antonioni-ism.”) Nevertheless, Rossellini gladly accepted a scenario credit and payment from Godard for LES CARABINIERS, a loose adaptation of Benjamin Joppolo’s anti-war play, I carabinieri. Rossellini had directed a stage production in Spoleto, in defiance of a government ban on the play, and his sole contribution to the film was providing an oral summary of Joppolo’s script, which Godard transcribed, cut up, and pasted in his notebook. Godard’s version lets two country bumpkins, Michelangelo and Ulysses, loose upon the world, their only directive from their military recruiter being death, destruction, and any other war crimes they can dream up. The duo’s atrocities are intercut with newsreel footage, postcards of plunder, and other Godardian digressions.

screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. screenings.description: Italy, 2020 Directed by Alessandro Rossellini Featuring Isabella Rossellini, Ingrid Rossellini, Renzo Rossellini, Robin Rossellini, Gil Nur Rossellini Approx. 90 min. “My grandfather left the world his masterpieces, and not a penny to any of us. Instead, he left us an enormous inheritance of family conflicts,” declares Alessandro Rossellini, the son of Renzo Rossellini and grandson of Roberto and his second wife Marcella. Between Roberto’s four wives, numerous mistresses, and descendants stretching from New York to Sweden to Qatar, the Rossellini legacy is nothing if not capacious. In this personal documentary, Alessandro interviews his relatives and tries to diagnose the roots of a genetic ailment: Rossellinitis. Characterized by conviction, outspokenness, and wanderlust (or just plain lust), those suffering from Rossellinitis are encouraged to look deeply into family history and discuss. Courtesy B&B Film.

screenings.title: Minotaur
screenings.description: Intrigue, corruption, betrayal, survival: the walls of the maze are closing in. The latest from Oscar® nominated writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan), Cannes Grand Prix winner MINOTAUR is a twist-laden parable for our times. Russia, 2022. Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence. A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

screenings.title: 14th
screenings.description: Written in the wreckage of the Civil War, the 14th Amendment was meant to codify the promise of freedom and citizenship. Instead, it has become a permanent argument. Oscar nominee DuVernay’s new documentary pulls this fight out of the footnotes and into the present, chronicling a vicious battle that has raged for more than 150 years. Threading deep archival scholarship with today’s headlines, 14TH brings together legal minds, politicians, historians and cultural voices to explore a question America still hasn’t settled: Who gets to belong?

screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1987. 116 mins. 35mm. With Matthew Modine, Adam Baldwin, Vincent D’Onofrio, R. Lee Ermey, Dorian Harewood, Arliss Howard, Kevyn Major Howard, Ed O’Ross. Wearing a peace symbol and a helmet marked “Born to Kill,” Joker (Modine) is a military journalist trying to maintain his cynicism and sanity during basic training and combat in Kubrick’s harrowing Vietnam drama. Unlike concurrent films about the U.S. involvement in the war in Southeast Asia, such as Platoon, Kubrick’s film is by design unemotional, taking as its main subject the dehumanization of the American war machine itself, personified in the first half by the abusive drill sergeant played by R. Lee Ermey and in the second by the mechanical, distanced nature of the violent battles themselves. Kubrick is presented with support from the Criterion Collection. But times are changing for Harry. His daily pickpocket take isn’t green bills and wristwatches, it’s credit cards and cell phones. And one unfortunate night, cryptocurrency and a handgun. THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

screenings.title: A Fox Under a Pink Moon
screenings.description: Sixteen-year-old Soraya is a strong-willed Afghan sculptor and illustrator trying to find a way out of Iran and join her mother in Austria. This subtly textured self-portrait, shot by Soraya with her cell phone camera and directed by Mehrdad Oskouei, interweaves Soraya’s illustrations with chilling scenes of her escape attempts, political news from Afghanistan, and videos in which she sings and dances, or shows the bruises inflicted by her violent husband. Through masterful cinematography often filmed in dangerous conditions – and the protagonist’s radiant energy – this empowering collaboration between an established filmmaker and a young new artist enables her to reclaim her identity. screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.title: The Flowers of St. Francis
screenings.description: FRANCESCO, GIULLARE DI DIO Italy, 1950 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Co-written by Federico Fellini Starring Aldo Fabrizi, Gianfranco Bellini, Peparuolo In Italian with English subtitles. Approx. 87 min. 35mm/4K restoration. Rossellini’s account of a brief period in the life of Saint Francis is as plainspoken and modest as its subject, an anti-hagiography closer to the mud below than the heavens above. Loosely inspired by Fioretti di San Francesco, a nearly-contemporaneous 14th-century collection of vignettes, the film was shaped into a bare ‘scenario’ by Rossellini and Federico Fellini, but the final result remains bracingly plotless. A series of parables that illustrate the moral quality of its characters rather than any scriptural interpretation, THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS is built from incidents and yarns: an encounter with a leper, a visit from Saint Clare, the quest for a pig’s foot, and the tale of the brother who keeps giving away his clothes. Francis is played by Brother Nazario Gerardi and the ranks of his disciples are populated by real-life monks that Rossellini featured in PAISAN; the only professional actor in sight is Aldo Fabrizi, with an extended cameo as a preening warlord. Financed by a credulous publisher who believed Rossellini would deliver a devout testament whose debut would coincide with the papally declared ‘Holy Year’ of 1950, THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS instead premiered in the aftermath of Rossellini’s unsaintly and adulterous dalliance with Ingrid Bergman. The initial critical reaction was indifferent, but Rossellini had the last laugh; in 1995, the Vatican named THE FLOWERS OF ST. FRANCIS among fifteen essential works of religious cinema. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà. 4K restoration courtesy Janus Films. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

Amidst the comfortable trappings of affluence and domesticity, corporate executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) finds himself under siege on all fronts. At home, he is haunted by suspicions that his increasingly distant wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is unfaithful. At work, he contends with a demand from local authorities to draft a quota of employees for the war in Ukraine. Desperate to keep his hands clean, Gleb struggles to reassert control even as the collapse of his carefully ordered life seems fated to accelerate toward violence. A pressure cooker in cinematic form, MINOTAUR uncovers and indicts the heart of societal darkness with searing clarity. Uniting intimately-drawn performances and stark visual power, France’s Best International Feature Film entry to the 99th Academy Awards® is peerless work from an indisputable master.

Salaryman Teruyuki Kagawa, newly out of work, struggles to keep up the illusion of employment for his family, consisting of one son who lights out to join the US Army, another with a not-so-dirty secret of his own (the scamp is taking piano lessons), and a wife (Kyōko Koizumi) who finds an unlikely solution to her unhappy domestic existence when she’s kidnapped by a home invader. Haunted by the memory of his young daughter’s abduction, he eventually strikes up a relationship with a young mother and her child (Amy Ryan and Abigail Breslin). screenings.title: New Yorkers + Before the First Word
screenings.description: This program pairs two films, made a decade apart, that vividly demonstrate the vibrant, distinctive, and sometimes paradoxical nature of New York City’s neighborhoods: at once strikingly diverse and worldly, and yet close knit and self-enclosed. NEW YORKERS (1971), by filmmaker Michael Blackwood (who during his long career made several films about the city, as well as dozens of documentaries about artists, architects, and musicians), sets its sights on the Upper East Side, and in particular on the area in and around East 77th Street. BEFORE THE FIRST WORD (1982) – a co-production between WNET and the educational organization Learning Designs, and ostensibly a film designed as a teaching tool for journalism students – is set seventy-something blocks to the south, in Greenwich Village. Both films capture the degree to which their respective neighborhoods have developed specific cultures, institutions, and local networks to create a kind of shelter from the vertiginous, unceasing forces of change that animate Manhattan – and the degree to which they’re nevertheless unmistakably subject to the evolution that is the fate of all city neighborhoods, and to the more aggressive, inorganic tides of gentrification that have increasingly transformed the city over the past fifty years.Michael BlackwoodNEW YORKERS1971, 29 min, 16mm-to-DCPTom SimonBEFORE THE FIRST WORD1982, 29 min, videoTotal running time: ca. 60 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: New York, New York
screenings.description: Dir. Martin Scorsese. 1977, 164 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Robert De Niro, Liza Minnelli, Lionel Stander. Scorsese’s ode to classic MGM musicals and 1940s jazz marked a departure for him, combining his gritty hard-boiled realism (he had just made Taxi Driver) with a celebration of the surreal artificiality of Hollywood. Undoubtedly one of the director’s masterworks, the film brilliantly depicts the difficulty of a marriage between two independent creatives, and Scorsese pushes the story of the doomed relationship between a jazz singer and a saxophonist into dark, exhilarating territory. The final half hour, when Scorsese gives the film over to pure movie musical magic, makes for one of his most sustained feats of grand filmmaking, while Minnelli’s climactic belting of the now-classic title song (written by Fred Ebb and John Kander for the film) is a true showstopper. screenings.title: Every Contact Leaves a Trace
screenings.description: “For most of her life, filmmaker Lynne Sachs has saved every business card ever placed into her hand – more than 600 fragments of chance encounters, fleeting conversations, and unexpected connections. Drawing on the forensic principle that every contact leaves a trace, Sachs selects seven cards and follows them back into the lives they represent. A German woman reckons with history, an artist reflects on government surveillance, a forensic scientist searches the cards for DNA, and when memory reaches its limits, cinema fills in the gaps. Blending documentary, speculation, performance, and personal reflection with remarkable grace, Sachs transforms an ordinary archive into a meditation on memory, history, and the invisible ways we shape one another’s lives.” –Bryan Wendorf, CHICAGO UNDERGROUND FILM FESTIVAL“Sachs reveals her strength: she captures beauty in the mundane, elevates the casual to poetry, and shows that even the most fleeting encounter leaves a lasting legacy.” –Martijn Smit, CINEMAGAZINE“Sachs extends the interpersonal scale of her inquiry into a more expansive awareness. Her on-screen interlocutors serve as mirrors into her own wandering mind, a gesture toward entanglement reminiscent of Chris Marker’s reflexive SANS SOLEIL. With Sachs, we learn that to be in relation is to come to terms with one’s capacity to do harm and to accept that we might leave imprints that elude our awareness entirely.” –Delaney Holton, SCREEN SLATE“A deeply personal meditation on memory, history, and chance encounters that exemplifies Sachs’s uniquely lyrical approach to nonfiction filmmaking.” –SCREEN MAGAZINELynne Sachs will be here in person for all screenings! screenings.title: Jane Elliott Against the World
screenings.description: The morning after Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, Jane Elliott divided her all-white third-grade class in Riceville, Iowa, by eye color. Her lesson in discrimination made her a national figure and a target. Nearly sixty years later, Jane Elliott Against the World finds her as funny and combative as ever. She stands with students, teachers, and families in Temecula, California, fighting restrictions on teaching race and history. At home, her daughters ask her to acknowledge what her refusal to stay silent has cost them. The woman who spent a lifetime asking others to change must now try to change herself.

screenings.description: At once a charming portrait of the diverse residents of a unique New York City neighborhood, a vibrant time capsule of the city at the very beginning of the 1980s, and a penetrating exploration of the social and political dynamics of a rapidly changing community, BRIGHTON BEACH is a long-lost gem of documentary cinema that has been newly restored by IndieCollect. Directed with great empathy and perceptiveness by Carol Stein & Susan Wittenberg, BRIGHTON BEACH captures the Brooklyn neighborhood known as the poor man’s paradise – a city by the sea down the street from the Coney Island boardwalk. Interspersing interviews with the neighborhood’s residents – including the Soviet Jews who had begun arriving in large numbers at the time – with archival footage of the area fifty years earlier, the film is both a portrait of a very particular time and place as well as a study of the ways in which urban communities function, cohere, and continuously transform themselves.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

Mann, whose “MTV cops” series Miami Vice was a primetime giant when Manhunter was released, recognized the crucial importance of a good soundtrack, and this one’s a doozy, with tracks from Shriekback, The Reds, and The Prime Movers, and Iron Butterfly’s “In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida” providing a needle drop for the ages.

screenings.title: Kaili Blues
screenings.description: Chinese filmmaker Bi Gan’s award-winning directorial debut is an audacious work that announced a major new filmmaking talent. Country doctor Chen Sheng sets out on a train journey to search for his brother’s abandoned child, only to find himself in a dreamlike world where the boundaries between past, present, and future—and between fantasy and reality—are porous. This remarkable visual achievement, which feels as singular and alien as the films of Apichatpong Weerasethakul, was shot in the mining village Kaili, the director’s birthplace, and incorporates poetry he’s been writing since he was a teenager.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. Distributor: Grasshopper Film

screenings.title: Home Alone
screenings.description: Penned by the beloved John Hughes and starring a young precious Macaulay Culkin, Home Alone shows how resourceful a little kid can be when left alone… with stupid burglars. When his large family forgets him at home, amid a frenzy departing for a Parisian vacation, Culkin’s Kevin McCallister initially has a blast on his own, ordering pizza and learning how to shave. But he quickly turns into a mini-MacGyver when confronted by two idiotic criminals. With booby-traps galore, the resourceful youngster cleverly outsmarts the bickering thieves at every turn while his mother figures out how to get back home.

screenings.title: The Band Wagon
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 111 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Fred Astaire, Cyd Charisse, Oscar Levant, Nanette Fabray, Jack Buchanan. One of the crowning glories of American musical cinema, Minnelli’s The Band Wagon is a triumph of the form, recycling the old backstage theater formula into a winsomely graceful celebration of the virtues of popular art. Playing a version of himself as an aging Hollywood star, Astaire leads a cast that includes Fabray and Levant, standing in for the film’s real-life writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green; Buchanan, incarnating a pretentious, blowhard actor-director à la Orson Welles; and Charisse, playing the ballet dancer turned show business ingénue she then was. The Band Wagon elevates these Hollywood traditions to new heights of technical display (“A Shine on Your Shoes”), self-reflexive comedy (“That’s Entertainment!”), and sublime visual poetry (“Dancing in the Dark”). screenings.title: Peggy
screenings.description: With live piano accompaniment by Donald Sosin Dir. Charles Giblyn, Thomas H. Ince. 1916, 70 mins. U.S. Restored DCP courtesy of the Academy Film Archive. With Billie Burke, William Desmond, William H. Thompson, Charles Ray. Though most of the films featuring silent cinema star Billie Burke (the future Glinda the Good Witch in The Wizard of Oz) have been lost, Peggy was restored by the Academy Film Archive in 2018. Starring Burke as an independent-minded, wealthy young woman from New York who causes a stir when she moves to a remote village in Scotland, Peggy captures Burke’s dynamism, joie de vivre, and comedic brilliance. Burke was also well known as a fashion plate, and this film showcases the actress in her trend-setting one-piece “Billie Burke” pajamas, as well as an array of beautiful clothing provided by some of the most renowned couture designers of the period, including Lucile, Lady Duff Gordon. This screening is presented in conjunction with Bard Graduate Center Gallery’s exhibition Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film (on view now until January 3, 2027), which features a short excerpt from the film. This screening offers the rare opportunity to see the film in its entirety, and it will be introduced by Goddesses in the Machine co-curators Michelle Finamore and Emma Cormack. Herald for Peggy, 1916. Gift of William R. Bogert, Jr. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: The Saga of Anatahan
screenings.description: Visionary Josef von Sternberg had once been a feared and revered presence on the Paramount Studios lot, but after one too many clashes over his obsessive perfectionism rendered him all but unemployable, and a falling out with Howard Hughes over his Jet Pilot, “Jo” went independent, directing, writing, shooting, and narrating this sublimely artificial picture, shot entirely on a Kyoto soundstage, about a dozen Japanese seamen stranded on a Pacific Island with one woman—unaware that World War II has long since ended, and that a little war of their own is in the making. A favorite film of one of von Sternberg’s students during his tenure teaching at UCLA, none other than Mr. Mojo Rising himself, Jim Morrison.

screenings.title: Blue + Chinese Series
screenings.description: Over the same, unceasing monochromatic sea of blue, Yves Klein’s patented “International Klein Blue,” the voices of Jarman and collaborating actors (including Tilda Swinton and Nigel Terry) read a poetic text by the director in which he muses on the physical and mental deterioration wrought by the ravages of AIDS, as well as the endless implications of the color blue. Jarman would be gone within a year, but he left behind one of the great final films, a vibrant work of courage and clarity in the face of oblivion. Screens with Brakhage’s Chinese Series, a long-contemplated short work inspired by Chinese ideograms completed in the filmmaker’s dying days.

screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Time Indefinite
screenings.description: His complicated relationship with his aging surgeon father, his settling into married life and fatherhood in early middle-age—these subjects, the sort of foundational building blocks of life so central as to often be taken for granted, are at the center of McElwee’s autobiographical documentary Time Indefinite, a film that brings a dry, laconic humor to its very serious meditations on mortality, family, and spirituality. “A rich and compelling cinematic experience… Conveys a sensuous appreciation of the physical world that is so acute that the environment is almost as important as the people… Communicates a sense of the elusive moment in all its complexity and richness being captured.” —The New York Times

Treating sex as a mere fact of life, Morita captures his subjects' personal lives with heartfelt candor.

screenings.title: Rains Over Babel (Llueve sobre Babel)
screenings.description: Dir. Gala del Sol, Colombia/U.S./Spain, 2025, 111 min. In Spanish with English subtitles. A retro-futuristic, queer tropical-punk riff on Dante’s Inferno, Rains Over Babel follows a band of misfits converging at Babel, a dive bar that doubles as purgatory and is presided over by La Flaca—the city’s Grim Reaper. Here, souls gamble years of their lives in hopes of outwitting Death Herself. Among them are Dante, racing to uncover his past; Monet, a ghost desperate to reclaim his body; Timbí and Uma, descending through hell to save their loved ones; and Jacob, preparing for his first drag performance. Acclaimed at the Sundance Film Festival, this love letter to Cali, reimagined as the mythical City of Maya, fuses magical and gritty realism into a vibrant, psychedelic universe of love, identity, gender fluidity, resilience, and second chances. Colombia’s official submission for Best International Feature at the 99th Academy Awards. New York Premiere Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: Paradox on 72nd Street
screenings.description: Over the course of three years, Gene Searchinger filmed pedestrians, joggers, buskers, bench sitters, stoop sleepers, and countless other types of New Yorker (whom the narration describes as “exaggerated Americans”) at the corner of Broadway and 72nd St. Visually, the film presents an hour-long stream of individuals, each with their own unfathomable inner mindscape, who together comprise “the collective”; the paradox referred to in the title is narrator Lewis Thomas’s assertion that, “It is in our genes to live together and to depend on each other, to be our individual separate selves and at the same time the working parts of others.” Thomas, a biologist and the film’s co-writer, shares narrating duties with the anthropologist Philip Slater, both of whom offer meandering philosophical notes on individualism in American society.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Every Contact Leaves a Trace
screenings.description: “For most of her life, filmmaker Lynne Sachs has saved every business card ever placed into her hand – more than 600 fragments of chance encounters, fleeting conversations, and unexpected connections. Drawing on the forensic principle that every contact leaves a trace, Sachs selects seven cards and follows them back into the lives they represent. A German woman reckons with history, an artist reflects on government surveillance, a forensic scientist searches the cards for DNA, and when memory reaches its limits, cinema fills in the gaps. Blending documentary, speculation, performance, and personal reflection with remarkable grace, Sachs transforms an ordinary archive into a meditation on memory, history, and the invisible ways we shape one another’s lives.” –Bryan Wendorf, CHICAGO UNDERGROUND FILM FESTIVAL“Sachs reveals her strength: she captures beauty in the mundane, elevates the casual to poetry, and shows that even the most fleeting encounter leaves a lasting legacy.” –Martijn Smit, CINEMAGAZINE“Sachs extends the interpersonal scale of her inquiry into a more expansive awareness. Her on-screen interlocutors serve as mirrors into her own wandering mind, a gesture toward entanglement reminiscent of Chris Marker’s reflexive SANS SOLEIL. With Sachs, we learn that to be in relation is to come to terms with one’s capacity to do harm and to accept that we might leave imprints that elude our awareness entirely.” –Delaney Holton, SCREEN SLATE“A deeply personal meditation on memory, history, and chance encounters that exemplifies Sachs’s uniquely lyrical approach to nonfiction filmmaking.” –SCREEN MAGAZINELynne Sachs will be here in person for all screenings! screenings.title: ACE Presents: Day Night Day Night
screenings.description: Before her epic My Undesirable Friends made Loktev one of the most-discussed figures in contemporary nonfiction, there was Day Night Day Night, the director’s riveting fiction feature debut, closely following 48 hours in the life of an unnamed young woman, played by an entrancing Luisa Colón, as she makes preparations to detonate herself in a Times Square suicide bombing in service to an unknown cause. Shot with remarkable immediacy and adroitness by cinematographer Benoît Debie, best known for his collaborations with Gaspar Noé, and lent a sense of subtly rising tension that reaches a point of near-suffocation by editor Michael Taylor, Loktev’s austere film—and its brooding, taciturn leading lady—exert a sinister undertow pull of fascination.

screenings.title: Full Metal Jacket
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1987. 116 mins. 35mm. With Matthew Modine, Adam Baldwin, Vincent D’Onofrio, R. Lee Ermey, Dorian Harewood, Arliss Howard, Kevyn Major Howard, Ed O’Ross. Wearing a peace symbol and a helmet marked “Born to Kill,” Joker (Modine) is a military journalist trying to maintain his cynicism and sanity during basic training and combat in Kubrick’s harrowing Vietnam drama. Unlike concurrent films about the U.S. involvement in the war in Southeast Asia, such as Platoon, Kubrick’s film is by design unemotional, taking as its main subject the dehumanization of the American war machine itself, personified in the first half by the abusive drill sergeant played by R. Lee Ermey and in the second by the mechanical, distanced nature of the violent battles themselves. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
screenings.description: This film emerged from city planner William H. Whyte’s years of research into pedestrian behavior and city dynamics, conducted as part of his Street Life Project. His research resulted both in a film and a book, both of which closely analyzed the functioning of public spaces in various cities, above all in NYC. The book quickly became a classic text within the realm of city planning, and remains beloved not only for the wisdom and elegance of its insights, but for its disarmingly unpretentious, no-nonsense, and often flat-out funny tone. The film version fully embodies all the qualities of the book, and adds one special feature: Whyte’s own voice. Sounding very much like Jimmy Stewart’s city planner cousin, Whyte delivers the narration with an often-self-deprecatory folksiness that’s charmingly at odds with the stentorian tone of most educational films. The film is also effectively a work of street photography. Whyte and his team’s dedication to observing – and recording – the actual behavior of city dwellers, and their sharp eye for the behaviors and gestures that are most revealing of city life, result in a film that is – almost incidentally – a classic city symphony. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES is one of the great films about that strangest of creatures – the city dweller – in its natural habitat.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Jane Elliott Against the World
screenings.description: The morning after Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, Jane Elliott divided her all-white third-grade class in Riceville, Iowa, by eye color. Her lesson in discrimination made her a national figure and a target. Nearly sixty years later, Jane Elliott Against the World finds her as funny and combative as ever. She stands with students, teachers, and families in Temecula, California, fighting restrictions on teaching race and history. At home, her daughters ask her to acknowledge what her refusal to stay silent has cost them. The woman who spent a lifetime asking others to change must now try to change herself.
