However things quickly take a turn for the worse as scenes go awry, actors drop out, and Anne’s prickly friendship with her lead actress becomes increasingly toxic.

screenings.title: Tokyo Sonata
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s reputation was made as perhaps the most formidable figure in the “J-horror” boom, so his about-face into contemporary-set shomin-geki melodrama à la Yasujirō Ozu was an unexpected—but not unwelcome—surprise… though beneath the placid surface of Tokyo Sonata, sinister stirrings are very much visible. Salaryman Teruyuki Kagawa, newly out of work, struggles to keep up the illusion of employment for his family, consisting of one son who lights out to join the US Army, another with a not-so-dirty secret of his own (the scamp is taking piano lessons), and a wife (Kyōko Koizumi) who finds an unlikely solution to her unhappy domestic existence when she’s kidnapped by a home invader. Winner of the Prix Un Certain Regard at the 61st Cannes Film Festival.

screenings.title: Taxi Driver
screenings.description: “Suck on this!” A pure distillation of needling isolation, inadequacy, and anguish, all roiling in the tortured gut of Robert De Niro’s insomniac cabbie Travis Bickle, who cruises all night through a stygian, steam-choked Manhattan, nursing his fears and hatreds. A defining picture of New York City in 1976, and a movie that is wrenched straight from the unquiet psyche of its screenwriter, exorcizing his personal demons.

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
screenings.description: “In 1969 the Department of City Planning attempted to shore up support for its various [development] projects with a multipronged, multimedia public relations blitz. At its center was the publication of a six-volume book, ‘The Plan for New York City’ (1969), which articulated the commissioner’s vision for the metropolis to stem the flight of the middle classes to the suburbs and revitalize urban space. The plan was presented in synopsis form as a propagandistic documentary produced by the Department and co-directed by John Peer Nugent and Gordon Hyatt. Featuring some flashy cinematography from New York location shooter-extraordinaire Arthur J. Ornitz [THE CONNECTION; MINNIE & MOSKOWITZ; SERPICO], WHAT IS THE CITY is an idiosyncratic document of the city in the late 1960s, offering a wide panorama of places and spaces, narrated by one of the plan’s ghost writers, William H. Whyte [THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES]. The film flits between footage of and discussion about ‘urban crisis’ (uprisings, poor housing stock, street violence) and purported city-led remedies. Viewed today, the film is both a curious relic of failed urban policy and an index of just how wedded city authorities were (and remain) to the idea that the manipulation of public perception is key to urban governance.” –FILM AT LINCOLN CENTERThe screening on Sat, Dec 5 will be introduced by series curator Lauren Lee White and producer, journalist, and curator Nick Fraccaro!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.title: It Follows
screenings.description: Mitchell’s Detroit-shot sophomore film, winner of the Next Wave award at Austin’s Fantastic Fest in 2014 and the breakout horror phenomenon of the following year, is a work of potent sexual dread, in which erotic congress transmits something much worse than a dose of clap: the attentions of a spectral, shape-shifting entity that pursues the afflicted with methodical single-mindedness, a pursuit that ends in terrible carnage. Enigmatic and unsettling, its thick atmosphere of paranoia incalculably added to by a soundtrack courtesy electronic musician Disasterpiece (Rich Vreeland), per Pitchfork “a score that announces when something is about to happen, only to suddenly upend expectations and leave the room on edge.”

screenings.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Classic Shorts
screenings.description: Along with the Academy Award–winning success of Aardman Animations’ 1990 Creature Comforts, it was this trio of inspired shorts featuring cheese-loving, jug-eared, Wigan-based crackpot inventor Wallace and his erudite pet dog/straight man/frequent savior Gromit that established the company as a stop-motion dynasty to delight all ages. Featuring A Grand Day Out, in which Wallace whips up a homemade spaceship in order to sample lunar cheddar; The Wrong Trousers, in which nefarious penguin Feathers McGraw employs a new Wallace patent in a daring heist; and A Close Shave, in which our heroes must step away from their window washing concern to foil a sheep rustling operation.

screenings.title: Poetry
screenings.description: Mija (Yun Jung-hee) has been tasked with raising her troubled teenaged grandson, Jong-wook, while her daughter, Jong-wook’s single mother, works in far-off Busan. When her capacity as a caregiver is threatened by a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s, Mija begins to study poetry composition at the local cultural center—first inspired by beauty in the natural world, then, when Jong-wook is mired in shameful scandal, inspired by new depths of disappointment and pain. Written specifically for Yun, a leading light of ’60s and ’70s South Korean cinema who gives an achingly vulnerable performance, Lee’s poignant, penetrating drama was awarded Best Screenplay at Cannes in 2010.

I’m sick of freight trains!’ both the romantic notion of the train and the idle fantasies of boyhood have been demolished. Suffering is everywhere and there’s no one to blame for it. screenings.title: Pinball (with director Naveen Chaubal in person)
screenings.description: With director Naveen Chaubal and producer Bryn Silverman in person Dir. Naveen Chaubal. 2026, 86 mins. U.S. DCP. In English, Arabic with English subtitles. In this tender coming of age portrait, Yosef, a spirited athlete in Louisville, Kentucky, contemplates his past as a displaced Iraqi refugee, his present as an immigrant trying to make sense of his kaleidoscopic identity, and his uncertain future. As Yosef reaches milestones of adulthood—high school graduation, his sister’s departure from the U.S.—long-buried questions come to the surface: where does he belong? Has he truly escaped from the shadow of war? What does it mean to build a future in a place shaped by the same forces that displaced his family? Is the life he is living truly his own—or simply the safest one available to him? In director Naveen Chaubal’s feature documentary debut, Yosef dives into the memories of his journey from Iraq to America and, like the steel ball ricocheting inside a machine, navigates shifting social, cultural, political, and financial pressures, trying to find stillness, purpose, and a place to land in an increasingly chaotic world. screenings.title: Jane Elliott Against the World
screenings.description: The morning after Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, Jane Elliott divided her all-white third-grade class in Riceville, Iowa, by eye color. Her lesson in discrimination made her a national figure and a target. Nearly sixty years later, Jane Elliott Against the World finds her as funny and combative as ever. She stands with students, teachers, and families in Temecula, California, fighting restrictions on teaching race and history. At home, her daughters ask her to acknowledge what her refusal to stay silent has cost them. The woman who spent a lifetime asking others to change must now try to change herself.

screenings.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
screenings.description: With filmmaker Matías Piñeiro in person The screening will be preceded by a book signing with Piñeiro at 3:00 p.m. Dir. John Ford. 1962, 123 mins. U.S. 35mm. With James Stewart, John Wayne, Lee Marvin, Woody Strode. Who shot the vicious outlaw Liberty Valance? Was it the law-and-order senator (James Stewart), representing the new order, or the rugged gunman (John Wayne), representing the pioneer tradition? There are no easy answers in this twilight western that serves as John Ford’s profound summation and reevaluation of his earlier movies and features Wayne and Stewart in two of their greatest late-career roles. The film that coined the phrase “When the legend becomes fact, print the legend,” The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is, per Richard Brody, the “greatest American political movie,” a truth-seeking frontier tale about the free press, vigilantism, and the myth of the American male. To celebrate the release of a new book on filmmaker Matías Piñeiro (Viola), The Originals is proud to present a 35mm print of John Ford’s The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, a film that Piñeiro writes about. Published by Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema, From where do you start when drawing a flower? is composed of Piñeiro’s notebooks, sketches, photographs, writings, and merges his filmmaking practice with his cinephilia as well as his longstanding work as a film educator. Writes Piñeiro: “As flowers are a motif in the title of my book, I could not help but think about one of the most beautiful flowers in film history: the cactus flower in The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance by John Ford. The beauty of this flower may reside in its extraordinary power for evoking a certain feeling of irrecoverable loss, a scar we have to learn to live with. This flower will be screened in a beautiful 35mm black and white print, as it was meant to be. The lack of color does something to this flower—we can’t learn all about it; we cannot fully pick it. It escapes us just in front of our faces but remains glowing within us.” From where do you start when drawing a flower? (Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema) Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: Leviathan
screenings.description: Setting out on the high seas of the North Atlantic aboard a Massachusetts-based commercial fishing trawler, Castaing-Taylor and Paravel produced one of the most mesmerizing, visually distinctive, and startlingly immediate documentaries of the 21st century, using the unique agility of their lightweight GoPro cameras to capture perspectives unlike anything theretofore seen in cinema, from gull-like views of the vessel to plunges into the slimy viscera of the day’s catch. “The density of aural and visual stimuli overwhelms—and liberates.”—Melissa Anderson, The Village Voice

screenings.title: Still Life + Train-Trains #2: A Bypass
screenings.description: A program of two formally adventurous trainspotting films from the Middle East. Stephan’s memory piece Train-Trains #2: Bypass follows the weed-choked rails of a former train line, an extension of the Orient Express that once linked Lebanon to Palestine, which lives on in the memories of those who reside near its long-abandoned stations; Saless’s Still Life, a key film of the early Iranian New Wave and winner of the Silver Bear at the 24th Berlin International Film Festival, observes the daily lives of a longtime crossing guard (Zadour Bonyadi) at a remote train station and his wife, whose well-worn routine will be upended by an unexpected development.

screenings.description: “This Emmy Award-winning documentary tells the stories of six ‘ordinary’ people who live or work along New York City’s Third Avenue, which runs for sixteen miles through Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx, cutting through the complex social strata of the city to reveal wildly different economic and ethnic subcultures. The subjects speak for themselves, offering candid glimpses into the disparate worlds of a junkyard dealer who steals cars, a Bowery denizen and the wife he abandoned, a welfare mother living in a condemned building with her five children, a sex worker, a devout Puerto Rican factory worker, and an aging Italian barber and his wife. screenings.title: The Celebration
screenings.description: The opening salvo in Dogme 95’s all-out assault on cinematic artifice, revolutionary in its emancipated use of the Sony DCR-PC7 Handycam, Vinterberg’s scorched earth melodrama/farce takes place during a gathering of the extended Hansen clan at a family-run hotel to mark the 60th birthday of solid burgher patriarch Helge (Henning Moritzen)—an event that takes a turn for the chaotic when Helge’s eldest son, Christian (Ulrich Thomsen), accuses his father of molesting both himself and his recently deceased twin sister during a dinner table toast. Abrasive, volatile, savagely funny, and endlessly inventive, one can scarcely feel indifferent towards such a blood-on-the-walls affair as this.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. screenings.description: Tarkovsky’s stunning, haunted sepia-toned sci-fi masterpiece follows a scientist and a writer who, living in a broken-down totalitarian dystopia, recruit the help of a “Stalker”—a kind of post-apocalyptic Sherpa—to guide them on a voyage of self-discovery, passing through the bleak, otherworldly Zone in hopes of finding therein a haven that will fulfill their secret desires. An enigmatic, austere, and utterly immersive experience that combines religious allegory and political prophesy, and has kept cinephiles debating its meaning for some 50 years.

screenings.title: The Inugami Family
screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Urban Video Project
screenings.description: “Urban Video Project (UVP) [was] a media education program [that ran] at Satellite Academy (Forsyth St.) from the mid-1980s through the 90s, providing students with the opportunity to craft half-hour documentaries as a cultural preservation effort, exploring the culture of Black and Latino people in their communities and the legacy of the African diaspora. Started by Salvatore LaSpada, a philanthropic consultant, Urban Video Project became integral to school culture at Satellite. It was emblematic of everything they were about: raising interest in learning and commitment to school through alternative pedagogy, hands-on, immersive experiences, one-on-one instruction, and allowing the students to be in control. […] The mission of these documentaries was twofold: to engage the students in school through media production, allowing them ‘to be the tellers of their stories,’ as LaSpada puts it, and to preserve the cultural heritage and current community of Black and Latino people in New York.” –Maddie DeLaere, XFR CollectiveThis program includes three tapes made by the students at the Lower East Side’s Satellite Academy as part of the Urban Video Project initiative, which have been preserved thanks to the efforts of the XFR Collective, Liz Andersen, and Salvatore LaSpada.NEW YORK, WEST INDIES: VOICES FROM THE JAMAICAN AND TRINIDADIAN MIGRATION 1986, 17 min, videoHigh school students of the Urban Video Project in New York City interview immigrants from Jamaica and Trinidad.EL PASAJE: RECOLLECTIONS FROM THE PUERTO RICAN MIGRATION 1986, 22.5 min, videoInterviewing the city’s Puerto Rican residents, the students learn about their history and the history of their classmates.EYES ON HARLEM 1987, 29 min, videoIn this tape, the students look at the community of Harlem in the mid 1980s as one of the legacies of the African Diaspora. They learn about present aspects of Harlem and the threat of hostile outside developers.Total running time: ca. 75 min.Introduced by Paige Laino (XFR Collective)!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Ascent
screenings.description: The bloodthirsty and seemingly unstoppable Nazi war machine is on the march towards Moscow in Shepitko’s wrenching, snow-swept World War II drama, which begins with two Soviet peasant soldiers foraging for food in a Belarusian village and proceeds to tell an emotional, lyrical tale of loyalty and betrayal, partisanship and collaboration, and, ultimately, the possibility of transcendent redemption. Shepitko’s final feature, frequently cited as among the greatest of Soviet films, won the Golden Bear at the 1977 Berlin Film Festival, just two years before its director’s tragic death in a car accident at age 41.

screenings.title: Les rendez-vous d'Anna
screenings.description: Akerman’s third feature was this transfixing—and, one suspects, quite personal—study of alienation and emotional withdrawal, in which a well-known Belgian director (Aurore Clément), traveling the increasingly homogenized cities of Western Europe to promote her latest movie, eavesdrops on conversations and passes through a series of brief encounters with acquaintances old and new, including a one-night stand with Helmut Griem, a reconnection with ex-lover Jean-Pierre Cassel, and a stiff reception from aloof mother Lea Massari.

screenings.title: Holiday Ghost Tales: A Benefit for The FOFIF
screenings.description: Screening of: Joanna Hogg’s The Eternal Daughter (2022) At an eerie hotel haunted by its mysterious past, an artist and her elderly mother (both played by Tilda Swinton) confront long-buried secrets.

screenings.title: Every Contact Leaves a Trace
screenings.description: “For most of her life, filmmaker Lynne Sachs has saved every business card ever placed into her hand – more than 600 fragments of chance encounters, fleeting conversations, and unexpected connections. Drawing on the forensic principle that every contact leaves a trace, Sachs selects seven cards and follows them back into the lives they represent. A German woman reckons with history, an artist reflects on government surveillance, a forensic scientist searches the cards for DNA, and when memory reaches its limits, cinema fills in the gaps. Blending documentary, speculation, performance, and personal reflection with remarkable grace, Sachs transforms an ordinary archive into a meditation on memory, history, and the invisible ways we shape one another’s lives.” –Bryan Wendorf, CHICAGO UNDERGROUND FILM FESTIVAL“Sachs reveals her strength: she captures beauty in the mundane, elevates the casual to poetry, and shows that even the most fleeting encounter leaves a lasting legacy.” –Martijn Smit, CINEMAGAZINE“Sachs extends the interpersonal scale of her inquiry into a more expansive awareness. Her on-screen interlocutors serve as mirrors into her own wandering mind, a gesture toward entanglement reminiscent of Chris Marker’s reflexive SANS SOLEIL. With Sachs, we learn that to be in relation is to come to terms with one’s capacity to do harm and to accept that we might leave imprints that elude our awareness entirely.” –Delaney Holton, SCREEN SLATE“A deeply personal meditation on memory, history, and chance encounters that exemplifies Sachs’s uniquely lyrical approach to nonfiction filmmaking.” –SCREEN MAGAZINELynne Sachs will be here in person for all screenings! screenings.description: Ingmar and Ingrid, Bergman and Bergman, together at last. Sweden’s most popular export before the Volvo, in her final screen role, plays a world-renowned concert pianist who returns home to reunite with her now-married daughter (Liv Ullmann), long a distant second to her mother’s career ambitions, the two women exhuming old resentments and struggling towards reconciliation over the course of an emotionally draining 24 hours. “So unrelenting, so harrowing, that I walked out of the theater on shaking legs. If you’re open to the experience that Bergman means to provide, you may leave the film muttering a wrung-out ‘Whew!’ followed quickly by an appreciative ‘Wow!’” —Richard Corliss, Time Magazine

screenings.title: Tickets
screenings.director: Abbas Kiarostami, Ken Loach, Ermanno Olmi
screenings.description: Bringing together the formidable talents of Ermanno Olmi, Ken Loach, and Abbas Kiarostami, the genre-hopping anthology Tickets presents three discrete but interconnected stories—involving a daydreaming Italian scholar, a brooding ex-soldier reduced to being browbeaten by a general’s widow, and an encounter between a pack of Celtic F.C. fans and a group of Albanian refugees—that unfold on a train travelling from Innsbruck in the Austrian Tyrol to Rome.

screenings.title: Bill Moyers Journal: Rosedale: the Way It Is
screenings.description: Amid the recession of the early 1970s, Black families began moving into nearly all-white Rosedale, a working-class Queens neighborhood just across the border from wealthy Nassau County. This film documents the explosive racist violence that followed: Tony and Glenda Spencer, a Black mother and father whose house was bombed twice but who refused to leave, anchor the film. “We’re going to stay here,” Glenda says. “Definitely going to stay.” (They did; as of 2019, she still lived in her home.) Moyers also follows a “home referral service” calling itself R.O.A.R. (Return Our American Rights) that aimed to keep Black people from becoming property owners in Rosedale, while moonlighting as a white supremacist terrorist gang. ROSEDALE was given a second life in 2019 when Sola Olosunde, a Hunter College graduate student in urban planning, sent out a viral tweet featuring the film’s most grotesque sequence, in which several Black children are assaulted by a group of white children. “Black and white alike in the Rosedales of America have been abandoned, condemned together to economic apartheid by a system that rewards the people who can afford to get out, and condemns to bitter, consuming rivalry those left behind,” Moyers opines. “It’s a travesty.”Introduced by photographer and public historian Sola Olosunde.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Taxi Driver
screenings.description: “Suck on this!” A pure distillation of needling isolation, inadequacy, and anguish, all roiling in the tortured gut of Robert De Niro’s insomniac cabbie Travis Bickle, who cruises all night through a stygian, steam-choked Manhattan, nursing his fears and hatreds. A defining picture of New York City in 1976, and a movie that is wrenched straight from the unquiet psyche of its screenwriter, exorcizing his personal demons.

I’ve not found out much about it since, partly because there doesn’t seem to be that much to dig up, but also because I’ve never wanted to disrupt its strange magic.” —Nathan Gelgud

screenings.description: Along with the Academy Award–winning success of Aardman Animations’ 1990 Creature Comforts, it was this trio of inspired shorts featuring cheese-loving, jug-eared, Wigan-based crackpot inventor Wallace and his erudite pet dog/straight man/frequent savior Gromit that established the company as a stop-motion dynasty to delight all ages. Featuring A Grand Day Out, in which Wallace whips up a homemade spaceship in order to sample lunar cheddar; The Wrong Trousers, in which nefarious penguin Feathers McGraw employs a new Wallace patent in a daring heist; and A Close Shave, in which our heroes must step away from their window washing concern to foil a sheep rustling operation.

screenings.title: Secrets & Lies
screenings.description: The winner of the Palme d’Or at the 1996 Cannes Film Festival, Leigh’s tender, funny, fearless film has Brenda Blethyn in a career-best performance as Cynthia, a white working-class woman who has a life-changing revelation when she meets Black middle-class optometrist Marianne Jean-Baptiste, who informs Cynthia she’s the little girl Cynthia had given up for adoption 27 years ago, all grown up. Developed, like all of Leigh’s films, through a process of collaborative improvisation, it’s a film of startling spontaneity and uncomfortable, unflinching emotional honesty.

screenings.title: Rashomon
screenings.description: A riveting psychological thriller and arthouse sensation starring Toshiro Mifune and Machiko Kyō which investigates the nature of truth and the meaning of justice, widely considered one of the key texts of Japanese—and world—cinema. Four people give different accounts of a man’s murder and the rape of his wife, which Kurosawa presents with striking imagery (those shafts of sunlight streaming through the forest canopy!) and ingenious use of flashbacks. Shooting the celebrated opening of his film—a torrential downfall at Rashomon Gate—Kurosawa and crew mixed water with black ink in the rain tank, creating one of the most sinister soaks in cinema history.

screenings.title: Black Women’s Hands
screenings.description: This program surrounds JOJOLO with depictions of Black women artists. Sarah Maldoror’s TOTO BISSAINTHE (1984) chronicles her long-time friend and co-conspirator, the titular Haitian singer, in both the exteriority of performance and subjectivity of the backstage. HANDS OF INGE (1962) celebrates the sculptural craft of Ruth Inge Hardison and was edited by Hortense “Tee” Beveridge, the first Black woman to work as a unionized film editor. The 1962 documentary is among the rich constellation of citations in Simone Leigh and Madeleine Hunt-Ehrlich’s CONSPIRACY (2022), a spellbinding mediation on the artistry, manual skill, and aesthetic labor of Black women across forms.Lebert Bethune & John Taylor JOJOLO 1966, 22 min, 16mm. screenings.title: The Sacrifice
screenings.description: Made when Tarkovsky was already suffering greatly from the lung cancer that would end his life, his last film is one of cinema’s greatest final testaments, a work that puts both pagan and Christian traditions of self-sacrifice into dialectic conversation. Shot in Sweden with renowned cinematographer Sven Nykvist and featuring several other Ingmar Bergman collaborators, including actor Erland Josephson, the gorgeous and deeply affecting film, winner of the Grand Prix at Cannes, takes place at a birthday gathering that’s interrupted by news warning of an imminent nuclear holocaust.

screenings.description: “A psychological drama depicting the birth and slow unraveling of a relationship within Montreal’s affluent bohemian circles. In this autobiographical debut feature – made in Quebec using cinéma direct methods and techniques – Claude Jutra reenacts his own romance with Johanne Harrelle. Set in the ‘open’ Montreal of the 1950s and 1960s, the film follows a young man trying to break into the film industry and a young Black woman – an orphan and a married woman – pursuing a modeling career. The two freely engage in a mutual confessional; this game of truth leads Johanne to question Claude about his probable homosexuality. They must also confront the agonizing dilemma of abortion when Johanne becomes pregnant. A slow unraveling of their relationship ensues.” –CINÉMATHÈQUE QUÉBÉCOISECLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
screenings.description: That the world of the future was to be increasingly shaped by Asia was a central tenet of cyberpunk, and so it should come as no surprise that one of the greatest of cyberpunk films came from the Land of the Rising Sun. Man and machine feel the urge to merge in Tsukamoto’s utterly indescribable midnight movie staple, an assault-on-the-senses body horror running of the gauntlet which centers on an anonymous salaryman who begins to transform himself into a man of steel, his waking nightmare captured in twitchy camerawork and lurid, gritty black-and-white 16mm. A symphony of sex, steel, and scarification, set to a scraping industrial clangor.

screenings.description: Serra’s visceral yet elegant documentary portrait of young, Peruvian-born superstar torero Andrés Roca Rey sees him risking life and limb on the clock, and in unglamorous off-hours traveling via minibus between arenas with an extensive, officious entourage. A privileged, patiently observed perspective on the flamboyant showmanship, ritualized grace, and terrible violence of bullfighting, that most controversial of the sporting arts, its time-honored spectacle of man’s cultivated, calculated intelligence facing down an elemental force of primal animal aggression, a spectacle that ends, invariably, in a welter of hot, bubbling blood. “Impressionistic and intimate… Perhaps the most immersive encapsulation of tauromachy yet achieved in cinema.” —Sight & Sound

screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn, the construction site manager, and Cal, a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone, Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Keane
screenings.description: Kerrigan, whose debut Clean, Shaven was one of the most harrowingly immersive portrayals of schizophrenia ever put on screen, dove back into the depths of a turbulent, fractured mind with the equally-if-not-more accomplished Keane, in which Damian Lewis, playing a mentally unsound William Keane, wanders the dingy corridors of the Port Authority Bus Terminal and other sordid pockets of New York City. Haunted by the memory of his young daughter’s abduction, he eventually strikes up a relationship with a young mother and her child (Amy Ryan and Abigail Breslin). A work of brilliantly sustained discomfort and tactile seediness, raw, rigorous, and entirely riveting.

screenings.title: Rex: A Dinosaur's Story
screenings.description: Released just two weeks before Jurassic Park and famed for the off-camera exploits of its director, flamboyant media mogul Kadokawa, Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story managed to do a brisk business at the Japanese box office, tugging heartstrings in telling the story of Chie (Yumi Adachi), a paleontologist’s daughter who discovers a Tyrannosaurus egg with her father (Tsunehiko Watase) and then forms an unlikely friendship with the hatchling that emerges from within. Made with a lavish budget that allowed for contracting the services of special-effects world megastar Carlo Rambaldi (E.T., Possession, Lizard in a Woman’s Skin), Kadokawa’s charmingly bonkers, Christmas-set blockbuster has now been remastered, primed to meet a new generation of international fans.

screenings.title: Castration Movie ⅗ Year of the Hyaena + Q&A
screenings.description: Castration Movie is a multi-part postmodern epic by visionary auteur Louise Weard. ⅗ Year of the Hyaena contains part of one chapter. In Chapter iii. Chastity No Exit Virtue Cuck, Michaela (Louise Weard) tries to be a good person.

screenings.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
screenings.description: Introduced by Kubrick archivist Michael Chaiken Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1968, 149 mins. U.S/U.K. 4K DCP. With Keir Dullea, Gary Lockwood. As brilliantly engineered as the space program itself, Stanley Kubrick’s mysterious and profound sci-fi epic—“the ultimate trip”—is about nothing less than the beauty and the banality of civilization, blending cool satire, an elaborate vision of the future, and passages of avant-garde cinematic inventiveness. Set in a future that is already the past, 2001: A Space Odyssey envisions space travel as both hilariously routine and mind-bending, a journey to the infinite and beyond that forever changed the way we see the universe and cinema itself. Kubrick’s surreal masterwork still has the ability to conduct viewers to untold, unknowable realms of artistry and daring. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Third Avenue: Only the Strong Survive
screenings.description: “This Emmy Award-winning documentary tells the stories of six ‘ordinary’ people who live or work along New York City’s Third Avenue, which runs for sixteen miles through Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx, cutting through the complex social strata of the city to reveal wildly different economic and ethnic subcultures. The subjects speak for themselves, offering candid glimpses into the disparate worlds of a junkyard dealer who steals cars, a Bowery denizen and the wife he abandoned, a welfare mother living in a condemned building with her five children, a sex worker, a devout Puerto Rican factory worker, and an aging Italian barber and his wife. This unsentimental portrait of the uncommon lives of common people is a subjective sociological study of survival in urban America.” –DCTVCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Straight Circle
screenings.description: A pair of enemy soldiers stationed on a remote border in a vast featureless desert descend into a state of profound disorientation after forgetting which side of the border is which. As they grapple with their identities, loyalties, and the absurdity of their situation, their isolation slowly gives way to an unfathomable nightmare that will blur the line between friend and foe.

screenings.title: Rock 'n' Roll High School
screenings.description: Dir. Allan Arkush, Joe Dante. 1979. DCP. The Ramones, P.J. Soles, Dey Young, Vince Van Patten, Clint Howard, Mary Woronov, Paul Bartel. There’s only one thing that Riff Randal (P.J. Soles) cares about, and that’s The Ramones. When the villainous Principal Togar (Mary Woronov) goes on a campaign to outlaw the rock music and confiscates Riff’s concert tickets, her only chance to meet her punk rock idols, the rock ‘n’ roll rebel and her friends go toe-to-toe with the scholastic sadist in a fight for control of “Rock ‘n’ Roll High School.” This joyfully absurd, Roger Corman–produced celebration of youthful rebellion pounds with the heartbeat of punk rock’s most influential band. screenings.title: Chronovisor
screenings.description: Béatrice (Anne Laure Sellier), a Columbia professor deep into research for a monograph on theories of memory throughout the ages, stumbles across the purportedly true story of the “Chronovisor,” a device said to be able to reproduce images from any point in history onto a television screen, and in short order her curiosity becomes an all-consuming monomania. (The genesis of Walker and Auen’s story is a claim by one Father Pellegrino Ernetti to have collaborated on the creation of just such an invention.) An ingenious archival conspiracy thriller that might have tickled Umberto Eco and Jorge Luis Borges, unfolding amidst the shadowy stacks of New York City’s libraries. “Wonderfully unclassifiable. A tantalizing armchair mystery steeped in occult-ish authenticity [and] a sly commentary on our own relationship to the pursuit of curiosity.”—Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Nocturama
screenings.description: Bonello’s ingeniously structured terror attack thriller opens with a group of tense, shifty teens prowling the streets and subways of Paris, in the midst, as it happens, of pulling off an intricately planned bombing plot. After the explosions, however, the film becomes something altogether different, as these pretty, vacant subversives tuck away inside a luxe department store and lose themselves in consumer culture—clothes, televisions, toys, and a stirring soundtrack that includes Blondie, Chief Keef, Shirley Bassey, Willow Smith, and Bonello’s menacing electronic score—all the while oblivious to the authorities tightening a net around them. A damning “allegory of nihilism and decadence” (Film Comment), fairly steeped in late Millennial malaise.

screenings.title: Simply Johanne
screenings.description: “Abandoned on the doorstep of a Montreal orphanage, Johanne Harrelle eventually rose to prominence as a gifted artist, actress, and one of North America’s first Black models. SIMPLY JOHANNE deftly explores her complex and audacious life through archival footage, interviews with loved ones, and performances of her writings by three contemporary actresses. The film chronicles the journey of a magnetic and passionate woman who defied the expectations of her time.” –LES FILMS DU 3 MARSCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: New Yorkers + Before the First Word
screenings.description: This program pairs two films, made a decade apart, that vividly demonstrate the vibrant, distinctive, and sometimes paradoxical nature of New York City’s neighborhoods: at once strikingly diverse and worldly, and yet close knit and self-enclosed. NEW YORKERS (1971), by filmmaker Michael Blackwood (who during his long career made several films about the city, as well as dozens of documentaries about artists, architects, and musicians), sets its sights on the Upper East Side, and in particular on the area in and around East 77th Street. BEFORE THE FIRST WORD (1982) – a co-production between WNET and the educational organization Learning Designs, and ostensibly a film designed as a teaching tool for journalism students – is set seventy-something blocks to the south, in Greenwich Village. Both films capture the degree to which their respective neighborhoods have developed specific cultures, institutions, and local networks to create a kind of shelter from the vertiginous, unceasing forces of change that animate Manhattan – and the degree to which they’re nevertheless unmistakably subject to the evolution that is the fate of all city neighborhoods, and to the more aggressive, inorganic tides of gentrification that have increasingly transformed the city over the past fifty years.Michael BlackwoodNEW YORKERS1971, 29 min, 16mm-to-DCPTom SimonBEFORE THE FIRST WORD1982, 29 min, videoTotal running time: ca. 60 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Scarface [35mm]
screenings.description: De Palma’s ultraviolent, ultra-quotable, ultra-colorful, ultra-everything remake of Howard Hawks’s gangster classic is the crass, visually loud flipside to the sober, muted The Godfather, a massively deranged and gleefully disreputable tale of the rise and plunging downfall of a Cuban immigrant turned Miami drug kingpin. Al Pacino throws himself into the title role with the fury of an angry Rottweiler, while Michelle Pfeiffer glowers gorgeously in her breakthrough role as his trophy wife. Featuring cinema’s second most shocking shower scene, a script by Oliver Stone, and a surging soundtrack by Giorgio Moroder, Scarface might just be the film of the Reagan ’80s.

screenings.description: The prehistoric and the state-of-the-art meet in Spielberg’s game-changing adaptation of Michael Crichton’s novel, which lays its scene on a Costa Rican island newly populated with regenerated saurians. The CGI was all anyone could talk about when it was released, but today you may notice the extensive use of sophisticated analog effects, and of course the peerless ensemble cast including Sam Neill, Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum, Newman from Seinfeld, and the “six-foot turkey” kid—the human factor that makes Jurassic Park truly timeless.

screenings.title: The Power of Kangwon Province
screenings.description: A film of narrowly missed encounters, effortlessly tossed-off beauty, lightly worn narrative complexity, and (of course) slurry, sloppy binge drinking, Hong’s bracingly brilliant sophomore feature, which premiered in Cannes’s Un Certain Regard section, follows the separate trajectories of a man and a woman (Baek Jong-hak and Oh Yoon-hong) traveling through South Korea’s ruggedly mountainous east, the two drifters gradually revealed, in their individual encounters, to be tied together by a shared past. “Etched with precision and conveying a world of feeling… One of the best films you can see this year… [Hong is] a master of ellipsis.” —Manohla Dargis, The New York Times

screenings.title: It’s a Wonderful Life 80th Anniversary + Book Event
screenings.description: Dir. Frank Capra. 1946, 130 mins. DCP. With James Stewart, Donna Reed, Lionel Barrymore. One of the most moving films ever to come out of Hollywood, Capra’s holiday perennial never ceases to surprise with the depths of its humanity and the force of its supernatural allegory. James Stewart sends the viewer on an emotional roller coaster as George Bailey, who dreams of getting out of American everytown Bedford Falls, only to find himself constantly drawn back in an epic struggle with capitalist fat cat Mr. Potter (Lionel Barrymore). It’s a Wonderful Life is exquisitely crafted, funny, wrenching, and in the end cathartic like no other movie. This special 80th anniversary screening will be introduced by journalists Emily St. James and Lauren Theisen, whose new book Every Time a Bell Rings: The Legacy and Meaning of It’s a Wonderful Life, America’s Most Beloved Holiday Film (Hanover Square Press, Hardcover), is the definitive cultural history of It’s a Wonderful Life. The screening will be followed by a book signing in our lobby. About the authors: Emily St. James (Woodworking) is a writer and cultural critic whose work has appeared in Vox, A.V. Club, New York Times, Vanity Fair, and Vulture. Lauren Theisen is a journalist and editor at Defector Media. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: Rex: A Dinosaur's Story
screenings.description: Released just two weeks before Jurassic Park and famed for the off-camera exploits of its director, flamboyant media mogul Kadokawa, Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story managed to do a brisk business at the Japanese box office, tugging heartstrings in telling the story of Chie (Yumi Adachi), a paleontologist’s daughter who discovers a Tyrannosaurus egg with her father (Tsunehiko Watase) and then forms an unlikely friendship with the hatchling that emerges from within. Made with a lavish budget that allowed for contracting the services of special-effects world megastar Carlo Rambaldi (E.T., Possession, Lizard in a Woman’s Skin), Kadokawa’s charmingly bonkers, Christmas-set blockbuster has now been remastered, primed to meet a new generation of international fans.

screenings.title: Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach
screenings.description: Renowned harpsichordist Gustave Leonhardt plays—and plays as—Johann Sebastian Bach in Straub and Huillet’s remarkable film on the composer, based in part on a fictional journal by his second wife, and built around live-sound recordings of Leonhardt performing in the actual locations where his works originally premiered. Explaining their unique and radical reinvention of the oft-clichéd musician biopic, Straub explained: “The point of departure for our Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach was the idea of attempting to make a film in which we use music, not as accompaniment, nor as commentary, but as aesthetic material.” The subtitles on this film was overseen and approved by Danièle Huillet and Jean-Marie Straub. The subtitles follow two unorthodox principles: they are as literal as possible and certain sections are left un-translated. This represents a break within the film with the notion that the meaning of a text is in the words and their interpretation alone. Furthermore, the passages without subtitles allow audiences a chance to hear and see the film without reading.

screenings.title: Pictures of Ghosts
screenings.description: Dir. Kleber Mendonça Filho. 2023, 93 mins. Brazil. DCP. In Portuguese with English subtitles. Acclaimed Brazilian director Kleber Mendonça Filho (Bacurau, Aquarius) turns to the deeply personal and the cinephilic in this multidimensional journey through time, sound, architecture and filmmaking. Using the urban landscape of Recife as backdrop, Mendonça weaves a tapestry of history and movie love, examining the great movie theaters of his past, spaces of community from the 20th century that are now halls haunted by the ghosts of the past. Combining archival documentary footage, clips from his own work, and memories from his childhood and adolescence, Pictures of Ghosts draws a map of the city with cinema as its north star. screenings.title: The Stranger
screenings.description: The coda of perhaps the most celebrated career in subcontinental cinema, Ray’s The Stranger adapts one of the director’s own short stories into a comic, poignant film about the upheaval in a middle-class Calcutta family’s home that follows the appearance of a man, Manmohan (Utpal Dutt, himself approaching the end of a legendary life in pictures), who claims to be a long-lost uncle returning from globe-trotting travels. One of Cahiers du Cinéma’s films of the year, praised by critic Vincent Canby as “a small, gentle, exquisitely realized comedy about, among other things, family loyalties and trust in a world in which traditions have been devalued.”

screenings.title: Jollof Films presents The Price of Forgiveness
screenings.description: In collaboration with Brooklyn-based Jollof Films, co-founded by Senegalese artists Assane Sy and Ahmad Cissé, and their pan-African cinema club, we present a screening of Mansour Sora Wade’s 2001 The Price of Forgiveness, an atmospheric and dexterously directed film fable that lays its scene in a Senegalese fishing village where the locals struggle to lift an all-encompassing fog that’s keeping their boats on shore, and two childhood friends vie for the attentions of the same woman.

screenings.title: The Clock (Introduced by Karina Longworth)
screenings.description: Introduced by author and You Must Remember This podcast host Karina Longworth Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1945, 90 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Garland, Robert Walker, James Gleason, Keenan Wynn. One of the great New York City movies, The Clock was made the year Vincente Minnelli and Judy Garland got married, and the film is a testament to their smashing collaborative artistry, just one year after Meet Me in St. Louis. Set over the course of one night and early morning, this lyrical romantic drama follows the whirlwind affair that blossoms between Robert Walker’s small-town soldier on leave, Joe, and Garland’s no-nonsense NYC gal, Alice, which takes them from strangers to lovers, and from uptown to downtown Manhattan, all in the course of 24 hours. In her first non-singing role, Garland finds all the right shades of longing, anxiety, and humor, while Walker is a poignant love interest. Minnelli’s exquisite first dramatic picture pointed towards a stellar career of dramas that mixed realism and romantic fantasy. screenings.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
screenings.description: This film emerged from city planner William H. Whyte’s years of research into pedestrian behavior and city dynamics, conducted as part of his Street Life Project. His research resulted both in a film and a book, both of which closely analyzed the functioning of public spaces in various cities, above all in NYC. The book quickly became a classic text within the realm of city planning, and remains beloved not only for the wisdom and elegance of its insights, but for its disarmingly unpretentious, no-nonsense, and often flat-out funny tone. The film version fully embodies all the qualities of the book, and adds one special feature: Whyte’s own voice. Sounding very much like Jimmy Stewart’s city planner cousin, Whyte delivers the narration with an often-self-deprecatory folksiness that’s charmingly at odds with the stentorian tone of most educational films. The film is also effectively a work of street photography. Whyte and his team’s dedication to observing – and recording – the actual behavior of city dwellers, and their sharp eye for the behaviors and gestures that are most revealing of city life, result in a film that is – almost incidentally – a classic city symphony. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES is one of the great films about that strangest of creatures – the city dweller – in its natural habitat.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Home from the Hill
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1960, 150 mins. U.S. 35mm print courtesy of the George Eastman Museum, lent by an anonymous lender. With Robert Mitchum, Eleanor Parker, George Peppard, George Hamilton. One of Minnelli’s most striking inquiries into wounded American masculinity, this Western-tinged, widescreen, Metro-color corker stars a brilliant and menacing Mitchum as the powerful Texas patriarch of the Hunnicutt clan, at odds with his son (Hamilton), whom he fears has grown too soft being raised by his estranged wife (Parker). Evocatively shot and art designed in burnished, deeply conflicted earth tones, Home from the Hill, adapted from a novel by William Humphrey, builds toward a series of emotional climaxes that provide a perfect capper for Minnelli’s incredible run of fifties melodramas. screenings.title: Panelstory, or How a Housing Development Is Born
screenings.description: In a sprawling, labyrinthine prefab housing development in Prague, already occupied but very far from being completed, exasperated tenants struggle with the malfunctioning fixtures inside while outside, they negotiate vast plains of excavated earth that turn to muck and mire with the rain. Depicting one day in the life of this disorderly community, a day rife with aggravations and jerry-rigged solutions, Chytilová’s stinging satire of utopian social engineering and the drab reality that follows its faulty execution drew the ire of Czechoslovak authorities, who held it back from exhibition until 1981. Panelstory remains today a too-little-seen highlight of a brilliant, unruly, and obstinate career.

screenings.title: The Sword in the Stone
screenings.description: Disney’s underrated adaptation of the first title in T.H. White’s classic series The Once and Future King relates the coming-of-age of a young King Arthur, here named Wart, and his training by the wizard Merlin. Using the Xerox-transfer technology the studio implemented to great acclaim in its preceding 101 DALMATIANS, THE SWORD IN THE STONE centers on the magical arts of transformation, culminating in an epic battle of Merlin against the evil witch Madam Mim.Preceded by:Georges Méliès LE MAGICIEN (1898, 1 min, 35mm-to-DCP)Like THE SWORD IN THE STONE, George Méliès’s LE MAGICIEN emphasizes mystical metamorphoses.Total running time: ca. 85 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Andrew Norman Wilson: Sound Works
screenings.description: Andrew Norman Wilson presents a selection of his disparate short works united by their shared attention to the aural, each beginning with or inspired by a sound, a song, or the spoken word. In a format inspired by VH1 Storytellers (1996-2015), the screening will be punctuated by Wilson discussing the manner in which sound shapes the creation and perception of his work. The evening’s bill of fare includes video art, music videos, narrative shorts, and the New York premiere of Silvesterchlausen (2025), exploring a little-known New Year’s Eve tradition whose origins remain wreathed in mystery, still practiced today in Switzerland’s most conservative region, the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

screenings.title: Straight Circle
screenings.description: A pair of enemy soldiers stationed on a remote border in a vast featureless desert descend into a state of profound disorientation after forgetting which side of the border is which. As they grapple with their identities, loyalties, and the absurdity of their situation, their isolation slowly gives way to an unfathomable nightmare that will blur the line between friend and foe.

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
screenings.description: “In 1969 the Department of City Planning attempted to shore up support for its various [development] projects with a multipronged, multimedia public relations blitz. At its center was the publication of a six-volume book, ‘The Plan for New York City’ (1969), which articulated the commissioner’s vision for the metropolis to stem the flight of the middle classes to the suburbs and revitalize urban space. The plan was presented in synopsis form as a propagandistic documentary produced by the Department and co-directed by John Peer Nugent and Gordon Hyatt. Featuring some flashy cinematography from New York location shooter-extraordinaire Arthur J. Ornitz [THE CONNECTION; MINNIE & MOSKOWITZ; SERPICO], WHAT IS THE CITY is an idiosyncratic document of the city in the late 1960s, offering a wide panorama of places and spaces, narrated by one of the plan’s ghost writers, William H. Whyte [THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES]. The film flits between footage of and discussion about ‘urban crisis’ (uprisings, poor housing stock, street violence) and purported city-led remedies. Viewed today, the film is both a curious relic of failed urban policy and an index of just how wedded city authorities were (and remain) to the idea that the manipulation of public perception is key to urban governance.” –FILM AT LINCOLN CENTERThe screening on Sat, Dec 5 will be introduced by series curator Lauren Lee White and producer, journalist, and curator Nick Fraccaro!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Suspiria [4K DCP]
screenings.description: A fairy tale construction at once grim and florid, Argento’s best-known film finds Jessica Harper’s American ballet dancer arriving at an exclusive academy in Germany where she discovers a dark past and occult forces at work in the present. With some of Argento’s most perversely ingenious set pieces, a plum part for former Fritz Lang muse Joan Bennett, and a spine-tingling theme by Goblin that will haunt you to the grave.

screenings.title: Wolf's Hole
screenings.description: Wolf’s Hole opens looking very much like a Czechoslovak take on the contemporary American ski chalet-set teen sex romp, with a group of hand-selected youngsters coming together at an exclusive skiing workshop… but by the time it’s wrapped up, Chytilová’s film has arrived a million miles downhill from the likes of Hot Dog… The Movie and Ski Patrol. Strange goings-on will be nightly occurrences at the titular getaway, the instructors seem to be conspiring on a sinister plot that makes the Stanford prison experiment seem benign by comparison, and as a creeping paranoia gradually overtakes the group, the sick comedy that unfolds inside the lodge turns as black as the powder outside is white.

screenings.title: Wizards
screenings.description: Ralph Bakshi’s anti-fascist passion project, developed over decades and released prior to his LORD OF THE RINGS, mixes sci-fi and fantasy to tell the story of a far-future Earth where magic and fairies have returned in the wake of nuclear holocaust. These forces of good must battle an evil wizard who attempts to control the world by reviving the forbidden technologies of war. WIZARDS is pure, unrestrained Bakshi, filled with freaky characters, psychedelic backgrounds, and hallucinatory rotoscoping.Preceded by:Tommy Turner THE MAGICIAN 1998, 9 min, 16mmWIZARDS is paired with Tommy Turner’s THE MAGICIAN, a transgressive take on the rituals of ceremonial magic.Total running time: ca. 95 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Paradox on 72nd Street
screenings.description: Over the course of three years, Gene Searchinger filmed pedestrians, joggers, buskers, bench sitters, stoop sleepers, and countless other types of New Yorker (whom the narration describes as “exaggerated Americans”) at the corner of Broadway and 72nd St. Visually, the film presents an hour-long stream of individuals, each with their own unfathomable inner mindscape, who together comprise “the collective”; the paradox referred to in the title is narrator Lewis Thomas’s assertion that, “It is in our genes to live together and to depend on each other, to be our individual separate selves and at the same time the working parts of others.” Thomas, a biologist and the film’s co-writer, shares narrating duties with the anthropologist Philip Slater, both of whom offer meandering philosophical notes on individualism in American society.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.title: Rex: A Dinosaur's Story [Easy Reader Version]
screenings.description: Released just two weeks before Jurassic Park and famed for the off-camera exploits of its director, flamboyant media mogul Kadokawa, Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story managed to do a brisk business at the Japanese box office, tugging heartstrings in telling the story of Chie (Yumi Adachi), a paleontologist’s daughter who discovers a Tyrannosaurus egg with her father (Tsunehiko Watase) and then forms an unlikely friendship with the hatchling that emerges from within. Made with a lavish budget that allowed for contracting the services of special-effects world megastar Carlo Rambaldi (E.T., Possession, Lizard in a Woman’s Skin), Kadokawa’s charmingly bonkers, Christmas-set blockbuster has now been remastered, primed to meet a new generation of international fans.

screenings.title: Art Cinema for Tots: Tales from the Forest
screenings.description: Born out of a commitment to the idea that it’s never too early to introduce kids to the pleasures of movies made outside of the commercial mainstream—and the suspicion that young audiences are often more open-minded and curious than their elders when it comes to such matters—Metrograph presents the latest iteration of Art Cinema for Tots, a celebration of handcrafted, kid-friendly films that reconcile the smart and the silly. In this edition, join us for Tales from the Forest, a quartet of films by venerable Russian animator Yuri Norstein, whose meticulous, slow-moving perfectionism—each minute of finished film is the result of untold hours of labor—long ago earned him the nickname “the Golden Snail.”

screenings.title: 7 Women
screenings.description: For his final film, the preeminent poet of the American West on screen lit out for the East, or at least a soundstage version of it—and eschewed his usual masculine ensembles for a decidedly more feminine group. Ford’s swansong takes place among a group of female Christian missionaries—Anne Bancroft, Sue Lyon, and Margaret Leighton among their number—in a c. 1935 rural China ravaged by cholera and ransacked by Mongolian warlord Tunga Khan (hulking wrestler Mike Mazurki), whose horde, including Ford regular Woody Strode, pose a clear and present danger to the ladies’ redoubt. “Ford brings a mix of rigor and playfulness, of something hieratic and something erratic, because he allows a bit of playfulness into the game and puts himself into it… The truth, in Ford’s films, is not at the end of the trail, but always before there has even been a road.” —Serge Daney

screenings.title: A. Rimbaud
screenings.description: The improbable life of French poet Arthur Rimbaud unfolds with all the shock and playfulness of his poetry.

screenings.title: Fear and Desire + Kubrick Shorts
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1953. 62 mins. 35mm. With Frank Silvera, Paul Mazursky, Kenneth Harp, Steve Coit, Virginia Leith. Kubrick’s first feature was long unavailable to the public before its revival at the 1993 Telluride Film Festival and subsequent restoration in 2010. Begun when Kubrick was just 23, this allegory of war follows four soldiers who capture and torment an innocent peasant girl behind enemy lines. Made for $10,000 raised from friends and family with a script written by high school classmate and future Pulitzer Prize–winner Howard Sackler, this formally and practically inventive film is impressive enough to have earned the admiration of James Agee, even if Kubrick himself would later dismiss it as “amateur.” Preceded by Kubrick’s 1951 documentary shorts Day of the Fight (16 mins, 35mm) and Flying Padre (9 mins, 35mm), his first films, which show the influence of his years working as a New York photographer. screenings.title: Unstoppable + The Lonedale Operator
screenings.description: “Sometimes equipment breaks down, bosses suck, or security falters, but the demands of the rail never let up. Unstoppable and The Lonedale Operator, each on their own side of a century, imagine the worst possible day on the job. The irony for seasoned engineer Frank Barnes (Denzel Washington) and the station operator’s daughter (Blanche Sweet), is that neither is properly employed: Frank was recently fired, and Sweet’s character is only filling in for her sick dad. Luckily for a perennially imperfect American railroad system, these two heroes happened to be around!” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: Afternoons of Solitude
screenings.description: Serra’s visceral yet elegant documentary portrait of young, Peruvian-born superstar torero Andrés Roca Rey sees him risking life and limb on the clock, and in unglamorous off-hours traveling via minibus between arenas with an extensive, officious entourage. A privileged, patiently observed perspective on the flamboyant showmanship, ritualized grace, and terrible violence of bullfighting, that most controversial of the sporting arts, its time-honored spectacle of man’s cultivated, calculated intelligence facing down an elemental force of primal animal aggression, a spectacle that ends, invariably, in a welter of hot, bubbling blood. “Impressionistic and intimate… Perhaps the most immersive encapsulation of tauromachy yet achieved in cinema.” —Sight & Sound

screenings.title: Killer’s Kiss
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1955. 67 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Frank Silvera, Jamie Smith, Irene Kane (aka Chris Chase), Ruth Sobotka. Years before the flowering of the American independent film movement, Kubrick wrote, directed, photographed, and edited this self-financed New York thriller about a down-on-his-luck boxer’s relationship with a nightclub dancer. Killer’s Kiss reveals the young filmmaker’s heavy debt to film noir: attentive to spatial atmospherics, Kubrick plumbs the depths of darkness in several seedy urban locales, including the long-gone, original Penn Station. The frequently spectacular results anticipate the ingenuity of his later work, as in a climactic sequence of fisticuffs nightmarishly staged in a room full of dismembered mannequins. screenings.title: ASC presents: Death to Smoochy
screenings.description: Idealistic Sheldon Mopes (Edward Norton) has always wanted to bring his character, Smoochy the Rhino, to children’s television, and when the top star at the Kid’s Net channel, “Rainbow” Randolph (Robin Williams), is arrested in a bribery scandal, he sees his chance… But as it transpires, hell hath no fury like a “Rainbow” Randolph scorned, and Sheldon’s sunny disposition will be sorely tested by his predecessor’s sabotage and the sleazy reality of the children’s entertainment biz. An acrid dark comedy, with DP Anastos Michos lending the whole affair an air of blighted cheeriness.

screenings.title: Tainted Horseplay
screenings.description: Three thirtysomething friends united by their sybaritic appetites for booze, sexual shenanigans, and other assorted hijinks—František (David Vávra) a restaurateur; Milan (Milan Šteindler), a veterinarian; and Pepe (Tomáš Hanák), an auditor—lead a life of feckless, reckless promiscuity… until a HIV-positive diagnosis hits the group like a nailbomb, rending old allegiances asunder and lowering a paranoiac pall over the trio. A stinging rebuke to boomer narcissism and the overindulgence of eternally extended adolescence, phenomena evidently as epidemic in the soon-to-fall Soviet territories as in Manhattan, London, or the 16th arrondissement, cast with members of Prague’s Sklep theater group, who bring to the proceedings a snarky vivacity.

screenings.description: A pair of enemy soldiers stationed on a remote border in a vast featureless desert descend into a state of profound disorientation after forgetting which side of the border is which. As they grapple with their identities, loyalties, and the absurdity of their situation, their isolation slowly gives way to an unfathomable nightmare that will blur the line between friend and foe.

screenings.title: Raye: This Symphony May Contain Hope.
screenings.description: RAYE is a songwriter, storyteller and occasional over-thinker. She writes about love, loss, faith, joy and the strange theatre of being human – often all at once. One of the world's most celebrated artists, the South London-born singer-songwriter made history in 2024 when she won six BRIT Awards in a single night, the most by any artist ever. Her Mercury Prize-winning sophomore album, THIS MUSIC MAY CONTAIN HOPE. showcases her evolution as an independent artist, songwriter, composer, producer, and arranger. Now, leading with 11 nominations at the 2027 GRAMMY® Awards – matching the record for the most nominations received by a female artist in a single year – RAYE has reached another extraordinary milestone. THIS SYMPHONY MAY CONTAIN HOPE. comes to theatres as a four-act musical odyssey through the seasons of life. Going far beyond the conventional concert film, RAYE draws you into a world of breathtaking intensity, where every lyric carries weight, every crescendo hits deeper and every feeling sits impossibly close. Exhilarating, heartbreaking, joyful and profoundly moving, it’s a cinematic experience that holds you on every word. Joined on stage by 117 musicians, RAYE performs THIS MUSIC MAY CONTAIN HOPE. in its entirety, reimagined through extraordinary orchestral arrangements. Filmed at London's iconic Royal Albert Hall in October 2026, the film captures a night that Rolling Stone UK described as “a spectacular symphony of salvation,” in a five-star review. Yet beneath the grandeur lies something deeply personal: a tangible connection between RAYE, the musicians and the audience, shared through moments of joy, heartbreak, hope and release. It’s a family affair too, with RAYE joined on stage by her Grandad Michael, her sisters Amma, Absolutely and Katelyn, and her Grandma Agatha. Brought to life by award-winning director Rohan Blair-Mangat, alongside GRAMMY®-nominated production company Aldgate Pictures, creative director Mikey Robbins, and musical director Pete Clements, THIS SYMPHONY MAY CONTAIN HOPE. is an immersive cinematic spectacle infused with big-band crescendos, theatrical storytelling, and the indescribable stage presence that is uniquely RAYE’s. At its heart, the film is a celebration of family, faith, resilience and the extraordinary power of connection. A triumph in every sense, it’s a testament to an artist who continues to shatter expectations, carve her own path, and remind us that music is indeed medicine.

screenings.title: The Magician
screenings.description: Long though lost until its mysterious recovery in the late 20th century, Rex Ingram’s THE MAGICIAN remains one of Hollywood’s most extravagant explorations of the occult. It features Paul Wegener as the hypnotist Oliver Haddo (a character modeled on Aleister Crowley), who seeks out the blood of a virgin for his alchemical experiments in creating life. The film is based on W. Somerset Maugham’s 1908 novel of the same name, which Crowley vituperatively accused of plagiarism.Preceded by:Kenneth Anger INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER 1969, 12 min, 16mmTHE MAGICIAN will be shown alongside Kenneth Anger’s dense and mesmerizing INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER, which features the Moog drones of Mick Jagger and the Satanic presence of Anton LaVey. Anger held Ingram and his films in great esteem. He claimed that his grandmother, a wardrobe mistress, had worked on a number of his productions; through her stories of the time, the young Anger “became fascinated by this other period when nobody talked on the screen and when there were these magical, mythical images.”Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Scarface [35mm]
screenings.description: De Palma’s ultraviolent, ultra-quotable, ultra-colorful, ultra-everything remake of Howard Hawks’s gangster classic is the crass, visually loud flipside to the sober, muted The Godfather, a massively deranged and gleefully disreputable tale of the rise and plunging downfall of a Cuban immigrant turned Miami drug kingpin. Al Pacino throws himself into the title role with the fury of an angry Rottweiler, while Michelle Pfeiffer glowers gorgeously in her breakthrough role as his trophy wife. Featuring cinema’s second most shocking shower scene, a script by Oliver Stone, and a surging soundtrack by Giorgio Moroder, Scarface might just be the film of the Reagan ’80s.

screenings.title: The Empty Man
screenings.description: One of the most original and visually striking horror feature debuts in recent memory—thanks in no small part to the air of ambient dread sustained by Anastas Michos’s photography—The Empty Man, a burgeoning cult phenomenon, follows burned-out ex-detective James Badge Dale on an investigation into the disappearance of a friend’s teenaged daughter that leads him into a hidden world of eerie idolatry, eldritch evil, and psyche-shattering terror.

screenings.title: Calamity
screenings.description: Earning the disapproval and incomprehension of father and friends alike, Honza (Bolek Polívka, a physical comedian of rare gifts who would become a Chytilová regular) leaves his university studies for a job as a train engineer in a podunk mountain town, confronting the institutional rot of the state-controlled rail system as well as the machinations of three women (Dagmar Bláhová, Jaroslava Kretschmerová, and Jana Synková) who each have their romantic designs on our slacker antihero. A sex comedy with a satirical stiletto hidden up its sleeve, its climax—involving the train’s entrapment by an avalanche and ensuing anarchy—a masterpiece of comic chaos.

screenings.title: Kaili Blues
screenings.description: Chinese filmmaker Bi Gan’s award-winning directorial debut is an audacious work that announced a major new filmmaking talent. Country doctor Chen Sheng sets out on a train journey to search for his brother’s abandoned child, only to find himself in a dreamlike world where the boundaries between past, present, and future—and between fantasy and reality—are porous. This remarkable visual achievement, which feels as singular and alien as the films of Apichatpong Weerasethakul, was shot in the mining village Kaili, the director’s birthplace, and incorporates poetry he’s been writing since he was a teenager.

screenings.title: Brighton Beach
screenings.description: At once a charming portrait of the diverse residents of a unique New York City neighborhood, a vibrant time capsule of the city at the very beginning of the 1980s, and a penetrating exploration of the social and political dynamics of a rapidly changing community, BRIGHTON BEACH is a long-lost gem of documentary cinema that has been newly restored by IndieCollect. Directed with great empathy and perceptiveness by Carol Stein & Susan Wittenberg, BRIGHTON BEACH captures the Brooklyn neighborhood known as the poor man’s paradise – a city by the sea down the street from the Coney Island boardwalk. Interspersing interviews with the neighborhood’s residents – including the Soviet Jews who had begun arriving in large numbers at the time – with archival footage of the area fifty years earlier, the film is both a portrait of a very particular time and place as well as a study of the ways in which urban communities function, cohere, and continuously transform themselves.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Film About A Father Who + Q&A
screenings.description: With a nod to the Cubist renderings of a face, Sachs’ cinematic exploration of her father offers simultaneous, sometimes contradictory, views of one seemingly unknowable man who is publicly the uninhibited center of the frame yet privately ensconced in secrets. With this meditation on fatherhood and masculinity, Sachs allows herself and her audience to see beneath the surface of the skin, beyond the projected reality. As the startling facts mount, she discovers more about her father than she had ever hoped to reveal.

screenings.title: Monty Python's the Life of Brian
screenings.description: Brian Cohen (Graham Chapman) is an average young Jewish man, but through a series of ridiculous events, he gains a reputation as the Messiah. When he's not dodging his followers or being scolded by his shrill mother (Terry Jones), the hapless Brian has to contend with the pompous Pontius Pilate (Michael Palin) and acronym-obsessed members of a separatist movement. Rife with Monty Python's signature absurdity, the tale finds Brian's life paralleling Biblical lore, albeit with many more laughs.

A pioneer of “scratch” or “direct” filmmaking, Lye used various tools to mark patterns, shapes, and images directly onto the film’s surface, and often explored the dynamic energy of abstract images propelled into life by lively jazz scores or Pacific-inspired rhythms.Total running time: ca. 55 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Godzilla
screenings.description: The O.G. kaiju, a walking volcano of a beast who can flatten a Tokyo neighborhood with a single sweep of his tail, makes his screen debut in this appetite-for-destruction smash-up from master of monsters Honda, a strikingly somber first entry in the franchise which links the awakening of the ancient Gojira to the imbalance of nature represented by the dawning of the Atomic Age. Catch this pop culture landmark the way it was meant to be seen in the original Japanese version, with all the destruction and none of the pontificating Raymond Burr.

screenings.title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg
screenings.description: Demy’s poignant, particolored, all-singing musical tracks the budding romance between ridiculously good-looking young couple Catherine Deneuve and Nino Castelnuovo. The discovery of true love is depicted in a spree of bright, playful springtime hues and trilling song, composed by Michel Legrand, to thrill all ages, only for the star-crossed amour to conclude with a white-out and the most wrenching Christmas scene in all of cinema: a steady fall of stage snow, a dash of tinsel, a gas station office pregnant with regret, a swell of music, and a heavenward lift of the camera. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: Imitation of Life
screenings.description: Sirk’s supreme tearjerker, this stealth investigation into race in America takes the form of a deceptively glossy melodrama, with bottle-blonde Lana Turner as Lora, a single mother trying to raise a daughter and start an acting career. But as the film unfolds with Sirk’s usual visual splendor, he undercuts his own main narrative, focusing more intently on the fraught relationship between Lora’s African American maid, Annie, and her mixed-race daughter, Sarah Jane, played by Juanita Moore and Susan Kohner in Oscar-nominated roles. (An unexpected visit by Annie to Sarah Jane’s classroom at Christmas time is but one of many devastating moments.) Arguably the film’s most eloquent review comes from none other than Richard Pryor, in 1959 serving with the Army and stationed in West Germany, who was thrown in the brig after stabbing a white soldier who laughed through an on-base screening.
