screenings.title: Fanny and Alexander (Theatrical version)
screenings.description: Spend the Christmas Eve of 1907—and the aftermath of the sumptuous celebration—at the Ekdahl family home, as seen through the eyes of two of the massive clan’s smallest members, played by Pernilla Allwin and Bertil Guve, in Bergman’s intimate epic of holiday warmth and wintery family frigidity. A tender but clear-eyed recreation of northern European bourgeois life in the early years of the 20th century, evoking both its nourishing hearthside pleasures and the pinching pains inflicted by Puritan self-denial.

screenings.title: Leonora in the Morning Light + Q&A
screenings.description: In the early 1930s, painter Leonora Carrington, a rebel against social expectations, joins the surrealist movement and its iconic figures like André Breton and Salvador Dalí in Paris. A whirlwind love affair with artist Max Ernst confronts her with her inner demons. During the war, Leonora flees to Mexico and finally empowers herself. Today Leonora Carrington is one of the highest selling female painters worldwide, next to Frida Kahlo and Georgia O’Keeffe.

screenings.title: Rewind & Play
screenings.description: In 1969, in Paris at the tail end of a European tour, Thelonious Sphere Monk, the pianist, composer, and Promethean force in mid-century American jazz whose recording career would end little more than a year later, sat down for a television interview with one Henri Renaud. From rushes of that tense, taciturn interview, as well as footage of Monk onstage, as eloquent in his element there as he is tight-lipped in the TV studio, French Senegalese Gomis forges Rewind & Play, part essay film, part performance film, a keen interrogation of bigotry and bias in the music world, and a record of a transcendent talent.

screenings.title: Eyes Wide Shut
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1999, 159 mins. 35mm. U.S. With Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, Sydney Pollack, Marie Richardson, Vinessa Shaw, Todd Field, Alan Cumming, Sky Dumont. Met with befuddlement upon release, the final film by Stanley Kubrick is now rightly recognized as one of the great works of modern cinema—as mysterious and perfectly unsettled as ever. Kubrick spent a record-breaking 400 days shooting this beguiling, New York–set erotic puzzle, for which he meticulously recreated Greenwich Village on a British soundstage. Then a Hollywood power couple, Cruise and Kidman star as wealthy Manhattan doctor Bill Harford and his gallerist wife Alice; after she confesses erotic fantasies involving another man, he embarks on a surreal psychological odyssey that sends him into the depths of the city’s shadowy sexual underworld at Christmastime. The film’s centerpiece is an elaborate masked orgy that has the uncanny feel of a dream. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Terence Davies Trilogy
screenings.description: Terence Davies did not have a happy childhood, and his early adulthood was plagued by guilt and anguish over his homosexuality. But film became his outlet for self-expression, and in this trilogy of black-and-white short films, Davies brilliantly laid out the anguish of his bleak early years. In CHILDREN, Davies faces homophobic bullies at school and an abusive father at home. In MADONNA AND CHILD, the adult Davies spends his days visiting his aging mother, and his nights pursuing guilt-inducing sadomasochistic sex. DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION allows Davies to imagine the circumstances of his twilight years and recall slightly fonder moments from his childhood. Though these brilliant films were underappreciated on their release, they announced Davies as a major talent who became one of the greatest gay filmmakers of all time. What better time could there be than the Christmas season to catch this unrelenting exploration of gay Catholic guilt and existential dread?“The trilogy did the rounds of the international festival circuits and was often seen – in the States in particular – as an unnecessarily pessimistic piece, receiving limited arthouse distribution as a result. In a ‘glad to be gay’ climate, the insecurity, guilt and downright loneliness so astutely expressed in these films was an unfashionable stance. Because Terence dared to show the pain of growing up Catholic and homosexual in working-class Liverpool in the ’50s and early ’60s, the films were not celebrated enough. Terence once told me that when he recognized his homosexuality he knelt in prayer for so long that his knees bled – this pain is conveyed in the spirit of his films.” –Jennifer Howarth, SIGHT AND SOUND, 1994CHILDREN (1976, 43 min, 16mm-to-DCP)MADONNA AND CHILD (1980, 30 min, 16mm-to-DCP)DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION (1983, 23 min, 16mm-to-DCP)Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Day She Returns
screenings.description: After years away from the limelight, a recently divorced actress (Song Sunmi) is on the promo tour circuit again with a new film, and it’s in the course of three meetings with journalists (and a single acting-class exercise) that we come to know her—through what she chooses to reveal, of course, but also through what she discernibly withholds. Distilled to its Hongian essence, it can be described thusly: black and white. Disgruntled vaping. Wry humor wrought from a bare minimum of setups and almost no camera movement. A great deal of day drinking and midlife self-recrimination. Rote repetition of phrases that, in their minor variations, reveal volumes. The absolute precision of inflection and expression that one associates with the best of short stories. A mystery that continues to worry at one long after the credits have rolled. The 34th feature film by Hong Sangsoo.

screenings.title: Forbidden Planet
screenings.description: Take the bones of William Shakespeare’s The Tempest, move the action to the far-flung planet “Altair IV,” and gussy up the proceedings in CinemaScope and Eastmancolor and you’ve got this triumph of high ’50s science fiction. Commander Adams (Leslie Nielsen) touches down on the remote planet to find the only signs of life remaining from an earlier expedition are Dr. Morbius (Walter Pidgeon), daughter Altaira (Anne Francis), and their mechanical servant. The iconic Robby the Robot would be an influence on much sci-fi to come, but no less impactful was the pioneering electronic soundtrack by Bebe and Louis Baron, the first fully electronic score for a major motion picture.

screenings.title: Batman Returns
screenings.description: Burton and star Michael Keaton’s first Caped Crusader film was a pop culture phenomenon; their second was no slouch at the box office itself, but an altogether spicier dish to serve to unsuspecting multiplex audiences: an unremittingly grim, gloomily gothic blockbuster featuring Danny DeVito as a grotesque Penguin, commanding a fleet of heavily armed flightless seabirds to raze Gotham City; a deliciously plummy Christopher Walken playing a corrupt industrialist who happens to share his name with the lead of F.W. Murnau’s Nosferatu; and an ideal foil/love interest for Batman/Bruce Wayne in the form of Michelle Pfeiffer’s slinkily SM-suited Catwoman, putting her stamp on the role for time immemorial.

screenings.title: Sorcerer
screenings.description: This is hardcore: Brooklyn crook Roy Scheider splits town and winds up in the sweaty armpit of backwater South America, taking on a suicide mission to transport volatile nitroglycerine across a rugged, pitiless jungle in two dilapidated big rigs with fellow hard-up hard cases Bruno Cremer, Francisco Rabal, and Amidou. Suffused with otherworldly visuals and a mind-blowing score by Tangerine Dream, their first for a US studio film—Friedkin had seen them playing a gig at a decommissioned church in the Black Forest and was an immediate convert—Sorcerer “remakes” Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Wages of Fear like Led Zeppelin “remade” acoustic 1920s blues: heavy. Not for the faint of heart.

screenings.title: Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach
screenings.description: Renowned harpsichordist Gustave Leonhardt plays—and plays as—Johann Sebastian Bach in Straub and Huillet’s remarkable film on the composer, based in part on a fictional journal by his second wife, and built around live-sound recordings of Leonhardt performing in the actual locations where his works originally premiered. Explaining their unique and radical reinvention of the oft-clichéd musician biopic, Straub explained: “The point of departure for our Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach was the idea of attempting to make a film in which we use music, not as accompaniment, nor as commentary, but as aesthetic material.” The subtitles on this film was overseen and approved by Danièle Huillet and Jean-Marie Straub. The subtitles follow two unorthodox principles: they are as literal as possible and certain sections are left un-translated. This represents a break within the film with the notion that the meaning of a text is in the words and their interpretation alone. Furthermore, the passages without subtitles allow audiences a chance to hear and see the film without reading.

screenings.title: The Muppet Christmas Carol
screenings.description: The first Muppet movie to appear after the early death of genius Jim Henson, and the most emotionally rich of them all, a revitalizing retelling of Charles Dickens’s classic tale with Michael Caine as a superb Scrooge, Kermit as Bob Cratchit, and a host of fantastic new creations, including the big, bumptious bonhomie-prone Ghost of Christmas Present (“Come in, and know me better, man!”).

screenings.title: Meet Me in St. Louis
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1944, 113 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Garland, Margaret O’Brien, Mary Astor, Leon Ames, Lucille Bremer, Tom Drake. In Minnelli’s bittersweet turn-of-the-century tale, his first color film and one of the greatest musicals ever made, a family contends with life, love, and an impending move from St. Louis to New York City. Minnelli deftly organizes the Technicolor palette around Judy Garland, moving seamlessly between story and song—and what songs they are, including “The Boy Next Door,” “The Trolley Song,” and “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas”—from one season to the next. Featuring extended Halloween and Christmas sequences that place it firmly within multiple holiday movie canons, the whip-smart wry and gorgeously sentimental Meet Me in St. Louis is an endlessly rewatchable treasure that cemented the popularity of integrated narrative and music in American movies. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Pather Panchali
screenings.description: Inspired by an encounter with Jean Renoir, in Kolkata to shoot his The River, and the neorealist films that had emerged from postwar Italy, Ray set out to make his debut feature, an adaptation of the 1929 Bildungsroman by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, a beloved classic of Bengali literature about the coming-of-age of a boy living in a Bengal village. The resulting film, shot over the course of almost three years, was a breakthrough moment for Indian cinema on the world stage, a tender and lyrical depiction of a rural family set to a soundtrack of classical Indian ragas performed by sitar virtuoso Ravi Shankar, with a marvelous feeling for how the elements impress themselves on country folk’s lives—see for reference the justly celebrated monsoon sequence, moving deftly from jubilation to tragedy.

screenings.title: Saturday Afternoon Cartoons: That Frosty Holiday
screenings.description: Stathes joins Metrograph the Saturday before Christmas with That Frosty Holiday, a cheerful selection of heartwarming tales of the winter season. Come enjoy a famous mouse playing Santa for orphans; a fun-loving farmer having a wild ice skating adventure with the local animals; a grandfatherly inventor bringing lots of Christmas cheer to a very sad home; the animated debut of a very well known snowman; a firsthand look into Santa's workshop, and other stories. Spanning the 1920s through the ’50s, this assortment showcases classic characters such as Grampy, Farmer Alfalfa, Popeye, and others.

screenings.description: During her family’s move to the suburbs, a sullen 10-year-old girl wanders into a world ruled by gods, witches and spirits, and where humans are changed into beasts.

screenings.title: The Nightmare Before Christmas 3D
screenings.description: Dir. Henry Selick. 1993, 76 mins. U.S. DCP. With the voices of Chris Sarandon, Danny Elfman, Catherine O’Hara, Paul Reubens. Jack Skellington, the Pumpkin King of Halloweentown, longs for something more in life, and thinks he has found it when he stumbles upon the brilliant twinkling lights of Christmastown. He then becomes determined to have it all for himself. Conceived and produced by Tim Burton and directed by stop-motion animation whiz Selick, this meticulously crafted fantasy, featuring Oscar-nominated special effects and a dazzling, tuneful song score by the great composer Danny Elfman, brings two holidays together and has become a staple of both Christmas and Halloween. We’re pleased to present this modern classic of animation in delightful, delirious 3D. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. screenings.title: Art Cinema for Tots: Tales from the Forest
screenings.description: Born out of a commitment to the idea that it’s never too early to introduce kids to the pleasures of movies made outside of the commercial mainstream—and the suspicion that young audiences are often more open-minded and curious than their elders when it comes to such matters—Metrograph presents the latest iteration of Art Cinema for Tots, a celebration of handcrafted, kid-friendly films that reconcile the smart and the silly. In this edition, join us for Tales from the Forest, a quartet of films by venerable Russian animator Yuri Norstein, whose meticulous, slow-moving perfectionism—each minute of finished film is the result of untold hours of labor—long ago earned him the nickname “the Golden Snail.”

screenings.title: Drama! Experiments! Brilliant Finale!
screenings.description: “Drama! Experiments! Brilliant Finale! begins with a documentary film showing a central scene of early cinema: the fairground. A drama in the same milieu follows, the first film in our series by Albert Capellani, who, in 1906, began to transform early cinema by introducing the art of mise en scène. (His innovative, practically avant-garde The Bell Ringer’s Daughter ends the program along with Gaston Velle's Tit-for-Tat.") Next, four films that reveal the experimental side of early cinema: experimentation with color systems in the Kinematograph test reels of Tartans of Scottish Clans, the genesis of animation in Humorous Phases of Funny Faces, a kind of proto-surrealism in And the Villain Still Pursued Her, and a mixture of different experimental techniques, including scratching the film surface, in Gaston Velle’s Victims of the Storm. It is important to note that experimentation took place everywhere—in France, the US, and the UK. With the invention of so many techniques, the early cinema period was the most experimental in film history, it’s a shame that it is so often excluded from the history of experimental cinema. Trip Down Niagara Falls is a representative scène de plein air, a 'genre’ that brings the wide world to audiences—here in gorgeous color. The final film, the above-mentioned Tit-for-Tat, is a vibrant scène à trucs (trick film) full of magnificent techniques, and one of the earliest films in history promoting environmental awareness, conveying its message in an incredibly charming way.” —Series curator Karl Wratschko

screenings.title: Ec: George Landow, Aka Owen Land
screenings.description: “The unique contribution of Land’s work lies in the fusion of intellectual reason and, significantly, the humor that distances it from the supposedly ‘boring’ world of avant-garde film. Having explored the basic properties of the celluloid strip itself in early works such as FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR…, his attention turned to the spectator in a series of ‘literal’ films that question the illusionary nature of cinema through the use of word play and visual ambiguity. His work often parodies experimental film itself by mimicking his contemporaries and mocking the solemn approach of film theorists and scholars.” –Mark Webber, TWO FILMS BY OWEN LANDFLEMING FALOON (1963, 6 min, 16mm)FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR EDGE LETTERING, SPROCKET HOLES, DIRT PARTICLES, ETC. screenings.title: The Power of Kangwon Province
screenings.description: A film of narrowly missed encounters, effortlessly tossed-off beauty, lightly worn narrative complexity, and (of course) slurry, sloppy binge drinking, Hong’s bracingly brilliant sophomore feature, which premiered in Cannes’s Un Certain Regard section, follows the separate trajectories of a man and a woman (Baek Jong-hak and Oh Yoon-hong) traveling through South Korea’s ruggedly mountainous east, the two drifters gradually revealed, in their individual encounters, to be tied together by a shared past. “Etched with precision and conveying a world of feeling… One of the best films you can see this year… [Hong is] a master of ellipsis.” —Manohla Dargis, The New York Times

screenings.title: Metropolitan
screenings.description: One of the most iconic New York independent films of the ’90s, Metropolitan is an irresistibly quotable comedy of manners and a tour through an Upper East Side peopled by teenage patrician debutantes and dandies. When bright-eyed downwardly mobile Princetonian Edward Clements encounters a group of contemporaries self-dubbed the “Urban Haute Bourgeoisie,” fresh affections and rivalries are forged, and the newcomer is introduced to their manipulations, cruelties, and endless over-intellectualization of emotions.

screenings.title: The Cat in the Hat | Shot By...
The Day She Returns
screenings.description: After years away from the limelight, a recently divorced actress (Song Sunmi) is on the promo tour circuit again with a new film, and it’s in the course of three meetings with journalists (and a single acting-class exercise) that we come to know her—through what she chooses to reveal, of course, but also through what she discernibly withholds. Distilled to its Hongian essence, it can be described thusly: black and white. Disgruntled vaping. Wry humor wrought from a bare minimum of setups and almost no camera movement. A great deal of day drinking and midlife self-recrimination. Rote repetition of phrases that, in their minor variations, reveal volumes. The absolute precision of inflection and expression that one associates with the best of short stories. A mystery that continues to worry at one long after the credits have rolled. The 34th feature film by Hong Sangsoo.

screenings.title: Hail Mary preceded by The Book of Mary
screenings.description: Denounced by Pope John Paul II and hordes of protestors and full-throatedly endorsed by John Waters (“my favorite foreign film since The Moon in the Gutter… hysterically funny”), Godard’s Hail Mary offers a contemporary retelling of the virgin birth of Jesus, with the Mother of God (Myriem Roussel) as the chaste teen daughter of a Swiss gas station owner, fiancé Joseph a cab driver, and the angel Gabriel arriving via jet plane. (As ever, no one shoots commercial airlines more beautifully than Godard.) Screens with Anne-Marie Miéville’s The Book of Mary, a study of an 11-year-old girl who, as her parents announce their separation, withdraws into a private world of books, music, and dance.

screenings.title: Crocodile Dose
screenings.description: On their first summer back from college, best friends Curtis, Jimmy, and Abe embark on a fantastical 24-hour odyssey of drugs and alcohol on their way to a house party hosted by Curtis’s ex-girlfriend, Jane. When their pursuit of hedonism leads to Jane and Curtis reuniting prematurely, Curtis is unable to handle his emotions and loses touch with his relationships and reality.

screenings.title: Rewind & Play
screenings.description: In 1969, in Paris at the tail end of a European tour, Thelonious Sphere Monk, the pianist, composer, and Promethean force in mid-century American jazz whose recording career would end little more than a year later, sat down for a television interview with one Henri Renaud. From rushes of that tense, taciturn interview, as well as footage of Monk onstage, as eloquent in his element there as he is tight-lipped in the TV studio, French Senegalese Gomis forges Rewind & Play, part essay film, part performance film, a keen interrogation of bigotry and bias in the music world, and a record of a transcendent talent.

screenings.title: Magnolia
screenings.description: A movie of unchecked, cosmic ambitions and desperate emotional eruptions, Anderson’s mosaic magnum opus takes place during an eventful day in the life of the San Fernando Valley, as viewed through the interlocked stories of an ensemble that includes two aging, ailing television-world figures (Philip Baker Hall, Jason Robards), two drug-and-sorrow-addled women (Julianne Moore, Melora Walters), two “whiz kids” (William H. Macy, Stanley Spector), and an eerily prescient Men’s Rights monster played by a dead game Tom Cruise, all united by spiritual sickness and the songs of Aimee Mann. The climactic biblical downpour of frogs, incidentally, is based on an actual, albeit very rare meteorological phenomenon. Animal rain! Look it up!

screenings.title: Stalker
screenings.description: Tarkovsky’s stunning, haunted sepia-toned sci-fi masterpiece follows a scientist and a writer who, living in a broken-down totalitarian dystopia, recruit the help of a “Stalker”—a kind of post-apocalyptic Sherpa—to guide them on a voyage of self-discovery, passing through the bleak, otherworldly Zone in hopes of finding therein a haven that will fulfill their secret desires. An enigmatic, austere, and utterly immersive experience that combines religious allegory and political prophesy, and has kept cinephiles debating its meaning for some 50 years.

screenings.title: Beauty and the Beast
screenings.description: Tale as old as time, song as old as rhyme… After lean years through the 1980s, Disney animation had a blockbuster breakthrough with 1989’s The Little Mermaid, and their follow-up, Beauty and the Beast, likewise featuring irresistible songs by the team of Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, proved that Mermaid was no one-off fluke—the House of the Mouse was back! Based on the fairy tale published in 1740 by Gabrielle-Suzanne Barbot de Villeneuve, Disney’s charming retelling introduces us to bright, bookish Belle; her boorish, preening suitor, Gaston; the leonine Beast, living in seclusion from prying eyes; a host of delightful animate household objects; and not less than three Best Original Song Oscar noms. Be our guest!

screenings.title: Journey to the Beginning of Time
screenings.description: Working with what Hollywood would consider a pittance of a budget, Zeman, the presiding genius of mid-century Czechoslovak animation, created this stunning sci-fi fantasia following four teenagers who, on an outing in the country, hop on an abandoned rowboat to glide down a river that flows into a mysterious cave, on the other side discovering a lush primeval landscape where stegosauri graze, ceratosauri hunt the stegosauri, and wonder and danger lurks around every corner. Seamlessly integrating live-action footage with 2D and 3D stop-motion animation, Journey to the Beginning of Time ensorcelled audiences of all ages around the world, its mixed-media marvels in no way diminished with the passage of time.

screenings.title: Gertrud
screenings.description: Based on a 1906 play of the same name by Swedish novelist and playwright Hjalmar Söderberg, Dreyer’s curtain call stars Nina Pens Rode as Gertrud Kanning, an unhappily married retired opera singer who’s pulled hither and thither by various suitors, steadfast in her faith in the power of love through many an emotional buffeting. Dreyer, whose dedication to patient long takes and shunning of cinematic artifice here proved divisive on the film’s release, would respond to his critics: “What I seek in my films… is a penetration to my actors’ profound thoughts by means of their most subtle expressions… not the technique of cinema. Gertrud is a film that I made with my heart.”

screenings.title: The Lost World
screenings.description: In between cracking out Sherlock Holmes mysteries Arthur Conan Doyle found time to pen one of the first entries in the dinosploitation genre, 1912’s The Lost World, adapted to the screen in 1925 with stop-motion effects by pioneer-in-the-field Willis O’Brien, who would repeat his success with animating tyrannosaurs in 1933’s King Kong. Prim Paula White (Bessie Love) presents London eccentric Professor Challenger (Wallace Beery) with evidence that sauropods and theropods still walk the earth on a plateau in an obscure corner of South America, and in short time they’ve mounted an expedition to that very locality, there to find themselves up to their necks in Triceratops and Trachodons and trouble.

screenings.description: Cinema Tehran presents Marjane Satrapi & Vincent Paronnaud’s Persepolis (35mm), adapted from Satrapi’s autobiographical graphic memoir. As revolution reshapes Iran, young Marji grows up amid political upheaval, family stories, punk music, and the pressures of finding her place in the world. Told in striking B/W animation, the film follows her from childhood in Tehran to adolescence abroad portraying a turbulent life lived between different cultures.

screenings.title: A Tale of the Wind
screenings.description: Almost 60 years after the completion of his first film, Netherlands-born Ivens arrived in China, where he’d first traveled in 1938—here the Gobi Desert, the Dazu Rock Carvings, the Terracotta Army, and the Leshan Giant Buddha all receive visits—to produce this elliptical, ruminative last will and testament comprised of “dreams, dramatized myths and real life” [The New York Times], effortlessly reconciling cinema’s documentary and fantasy traditions. The story of a life spent, in Ivens’s words, trying to “tame the wind and harness the sea,” and a strikingly calm goodbye from a filmmaker who spent so much time focusing on the seemingly ceaseless upheavals of the 20th century.

screenings.title: The Day He Arrives
screenings.description: On the first night of a visit to Seoul, where he formerly lived, Sungjoon (Yu Junsang), a onetime film director who’s scuttled into a cozy academic sinecure, gets catastrophically drunk with a pack of students and pays a tearful visit to an ex-girlfriend (Kim Bokyung). Thus begins a four-day bender/odyssey of snowy, regret-riddled outings spent with old friend Youngho (Kim Sang-joong), Youngho’s alluring colleague, Boram (Song Sunmi), and a bar proprietress who’s a dead ringer for his ex (Kim Bokyung, again)—evenings that, like the piano piece Sungjoon plays night after night, are always the same, yet always different. If you are looking for one film that encapsulates the subtle delights of Hong’s rueful, deliberately minor-key art, look no further.

screenings.title: Ec: Christopher Maclaine
screenings.description: “The few facts that are known about Maclaine are, at best, sketchy. He was a published poet, a sort of down and out San Francisco bohemian who later became one of the psychic casualties of that scene. His last years were spent at Sunnyacres, a state mental hospital in Fairfield, California. These films, along with Ron Rice’s, are clearly the most significant work to come out of the beat period.” –J.J. screenings.title: Godzilla
screenings.description: The O.G. kaiju, a walking volcano of a beast who can flatten a Tokyo neighborhood with a single sweep of his tail, makes his screen debut in this appetite-for-destruction smash-up from master of monsters Honda, a strikingly somber first entry in the franchise which links the awakening of the ancient Gojira to the imbalance of nature represented by the dawning of the Atomic Age. Catch this pop culture landmark the way it was meant to be seen in the original Japanese version, with all the destruction and none of the pontificating Raymond Burr.

screenings.title: Empathy and Disaster
screenings.description: “The films of Empathy and Disaster depict events in the real world—or a staged re-enactment of them. Both create an immediate experience of reality, and stir feelings of empathy, regardless of how the images on the screen, ‘real’ or ‘fictional,’ were created. Today’s viewers should consider that one of the characteristics of early cinema is that it had not yet been standardized and sanitized, and therefore images that might, according to contemporary norms, be considered too crude were often uncensored. This program illuminates the fact that evoking empathy in an audience is one of the foremost aims of cinema, and had indeed already been perfected by 1906. It also shows that the boundary between nonfiction and fiction was already very porous in early cinema, and that much of what we now regard as a ‘hybrid’ film form has its origins in early cinema (e.g. The Alps by Telescope).” —Series curator Karl Wratschko

screenings.title: Isaiah's Phone + Q&A
screenings.description: A socially awkward high school student films himself as he blunders through attempts to make friends, spiraling into a dark place where his only close relationship is with his phone.

screenings.title: Sorcerer
screenings.description: This is hardcore: Brooklyn crook Roy Scheider splits town and winds up in the sweaty armpit of backwater South America, taking on a suicide mission to transport volatile nitroglycerine across a rugged, pitiless jungle in two dilapidated big rigs with fellow hard-up hard cases Bruno Cremer, Francisco Rabal, and Amidou. Suffused with otherworldly visuals and a mind-blowing score by Tangerine Dream, their first for a US studio film—Friedkin had seen them playing a gig at a decommissioned church in the Black Forest and was an immediate convert—Sorcerer “remakes” Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Wages of Fear like Led Zeppelin “remade” acoustic 1920s blues: heavy. Not for the faint of heart.

screenings.title: King Kong
screenings.director: Merian C. Cooper, Ernest B. Schoedsack
screenings.description: All aboard for Skull Island! The spectacle to end all spectacles featuring special effects that are actually special, it would require the visionary brilliance of stop-motion animation pioneer Willis O’Brien to bring the mighty Kong to life, and top-of-the-line c. 1933 military technology to peel him off the top of the Empire State Building. Featuring Fay Wray as the beauty who calms the beast, King Kong created the kaiju avant la lettre, the original and remaining undefeated champ of giant monsters running amok.

When one writes diaries, it’s a retrospective process: you sit down, you look back at your day, and you write it all down. screenings.title: Beauty and the Beast
screenings.description: Tale as old as time, song as old as rhyme… After lean years through the 1980s, Disney animation had a blockbuster breakthrough with 1989’s The Little Mermaid, and their follow-up, Beauty and the Beast, likewise featuring irresistible songs by the team of Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, proved that Mermaid was no one-off fluke—the House of the Mouse was back! Based on the fairy tale published in 1740 by Gabrielle-Suzanne Barbot de Villeneuve, Disney’s charming retelling introduces us to bright, bookish Belle; her boorish, preening suitor, Gaston; the leonine Beast, living in seclusion from prying eyes; a host of delightful animate household objects; and not less than three Best Original Song Oscar noms. Be our guest!

screenings.title: The Land Before Time
screenings.description: Fleeing natural disaster and the menacing jaws of the terrible Tyrannosaurus Sharptooth, baby Apatosaurus Littlefoot leads a party of diverse little dinos in search of their surviving family members and eventual safety in the Great Valley. A hit for producer Steven Spielberg and animator Bluth, the biggest domestic rival to Walt Disney in the feature game since the days of the Fleischer Bros., it’s ripe to be discovered by a new generation of young viewers.

screenings.title: The Thin Man
screenings.description: One of the most sparkling and convivial comedies ever made, this buoyant and bibulous wonder, based on Dashiell Hammett’s novel of the same name, introduced the public to William Powell and Myrna Loy’s Nick and Nora Charles—a rich, wry, and riotously drunk married couple who in their spare time get caught up in mysteries—as well as to their wirehaired terrier, Asta. Holiday cheer abounds as Nick shoots the ornaments off a Christmas tree with an air-gun gifted to him by his loving wife, one of innumerable brilliant bits of business herein; try to keep up with the Charleses martini for martini and you’ll be walking on your knees by the time the credits roll.

screenings.title: The Gold Rush
screenings.description: The second feature that Chaplin released under the aegis of United Artists, the studio he’d co-founded with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks, and D.W. Griffith in 1919, The Gold Rush was made with the writer-director-star’s total creative control, and as a result his film, concerning The Tramp’s holing up with prospector Mack Swain to pan for gold in turn-of-the-last-century Alaska, is stuffed to bursting with memorable bits of business: the lopsided cabin perched on the edge of eternity, the dancing bread rolls, Chaplin’s transformation into a giant chicken and yes, of course, that delectable shoe. “A comedy with streaks of poetry, pathos, tenderness, linked with brusqueness and boisterousness. It is the outstanding gem of all Chaplin's pictures.” —The New York Times

screenings.title: Rex: A Dinosaur's Story [Easy Reader Version]
screenings.description: Released just two weeks before Jurassic Park and famed for the off-camera exploits of its director, flamboyant media mogul Kadokawa, Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story managed to do a brisk business at the Japanese box office, tugging heartstrings in telling the story of Chie (Yumi Adachi), a paleontologist’s daughter who discovers a Tyrannosaurus egg with her father (Tsunehiko Watase) and then forms an unlikely friendship with the hatchling that emerges from within. Made with a lavish budget that allowed for contracting the services of special-effects world megastar Carlo Rambaldi (E.T., Possession, Lizard in a Woman’s Skin), Kadokawa’s charmingly bonkers, Christmas-set blockbuster has now been remastered, primed to meet a new generation of international fans.

screenings.title: Hail Mary preceded by The Book of Mary
screenings.description: Denounced by Pope John Paul II and hordes of protestors and full-throatedly endorsed by John Waters (“my favorite foreign film since The Moon in the Gutter… hysterically funny”), Godard’s Hail Mary offers a contemporary retelling of the virgin birth of Jesus, with the Mother of God (Myriem Roussel) as the chaste teen daughter of a Swiss gas station owner, fiancé Joseph a cab driver, and the angel Gabriel arriving via jet plane. (As ever, no one shoots commercial airlines more beautifully than Godard.) Screens with Anne-Marie Miéville’s The Book of Mary, a study of an 11-year-old girl who, as her parents announce their separation, withdraws into a private world of books, music, and dance.

screenings.title: Black Narcissus
screenings.description: A group of missionary nuns led by young Mother Superior Deborah Kerr set up a convent school in the Himalayas—in fact, whipped up at Pinewood Studios in England—but soon find themselves vulnerable to the howling winds… and other temptations. Ravishingly photographed by master cinematographer Jack Cardiff, Black Narcissus builds to near psychedelic delirium in a climax involving Kathleen Byron’s Sister Ruth, driven to the edge by unfulfilled desire for dashing station agent David Farrar, whose sloshed bellowing of “The First Noel” at a Christmas service while wearing the biggest fur coat you’ve ever seen appears a potent vision of spirited seasonal cheer.

screenings.title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg
screenings.description: Demy’s poignant, particolored, all-singing musical tracks the budding romance between ridiculously good-looking young couple Catherine Deneuve and Nino Castelnuovo. The discovery of true love is depicted in a spree of bright, playful springtime hues and trilling song, composed by Michel Legrand, to thrill all ages, only for the star-crossed amour to conclude with a white-out and the most wrenching Christmas scene in all of cinema: a steady fall of stage snow, a dash of tinsel, a gas station office pregnant with regret, a swell of music, and a heavenward lift of the camera. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: Carol [35mm]
screenings.description: A Metrograph holiday tradition, back by popular demand. It starts at Frankenberg’s department store, and an exchange of glances between Carol and the girl behind the counter (Cate Blanchett and Rooney Mara, both sublime), a look that tangles up fantasies of commercial acquisition and desire. What follows is maybe the finest romance this century has yet produced, an agonizingly slow seduction where the act of shopping for and decorating a Christmas tree becomes an intensely erotic act, and delayed consummation is packed with all the anticipation that a child has for finally unwrapping a present.

screenings.title: A Tale of Winter
screenings.description: This second film in its director’s “Tales of the Four Seasons” cycle draws inspiration from Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale while boasting of a grace and plainspoken beauty, and a reconciliation of philosophy and feeling that belong to Rohmer alone. Raising a daughter conceived during a brief but unforgettable fling, hairdresser Félicie (Charlotte Véry)—come Christmas season some five years after that fateful encounter—is found vacillating between two suitors while really loving neither, keeping a candle quietly burning for the father of her child and holding out hope that the New Year will bring her a miracle. “A nearly perfect work, in performance as well as execution.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, The Chicago Reader

screenings.title: My Neighbor Totoro
screenings.description: Two young sisters move to the country with their father and discover that the surrounding forests are home to a race of big, adorably plush beings called Totoros, who take them on a trip on a furry Cheshire Cat-like Catbus. A delight from beginning to end, and an international success that made Miyazaki a household name. Preparing the film, the director wrote: “My Neighbor Totoro aims to be a happy and heartwarming film, a film that lets the audience go home with pleasant, glad feelings. Lovers will feel each other to be more precious, parents will fondly recall their childhoods, and children will start exploring the thickets behind shrines and climbing trees to try to find a Totoro. This is the kind of film I want to make.” He did it, all right.

screenings.title: Imitation of Life
screenings.description: Sirk’s supreme tearjerker, this stealth investigation into race in America takes the form of a deceptively glossy melodrama, with bottle-blonde Lana Turner as Lora, a single mother trying to raise a daughter and start an acting career. But as the film unfolds with Sirk’s usual visual splendor, he undercuts his own main narrative, focusing more intently on the fraught relationship between Lora’s African American maid, Annie, and her mixed-race daughter, Sarah Jane, played by Juanita Moore and Susan Kohner in Oscar-nominated roles. (An unexpected visit by Annie to Sarah Jane’s classroom at Christmas time is but one of many devastating moments.) Arguably the film’s most eloquent review comes from none other than Richard Pryor, in 1959 serving with the Army and stationed in West Germany, who was thrown in the brig after stabbing a white soldier who laughed through an on-base screening.

Murnau’s Nosferatu; and an ideal foil/love interest for Batman/Bruce Wayne in the form of Michelle Pfeiffer’s slinkily SM-suited Catwoman, putting her stamp on the role for time immemorial.

screenings.title: Thief
screenings.description: Working with a deceptively simple premise—safecracker James Caan wants to settle down, but first he needs one last big score—Mann’s theatrical feature debut revolutionized the American action movie, fusing a detail-oriented documentary impulse, evident in its how-to heist scenes and casting of real-life cops and cons (Dennis Farina and John Santucci, respectively), with a lavish, pop-operatic style, with Mann turning the city of Chicago into a mythic, rain-slicked version of itself and a massive, immersive score courtesy Tangerine Dream. Disarmingly tender in its famed coffee shop monologue, scorched-earth savage when it turns to vengeance, Thief is a dab-handed genre piece that packs the heft of true tragedy.

screenings.title: Eyes Wide Shut
screenings.description: Christmas lights take on a malevolent gleam in Kubrick’s final masterpiece, a free adaptation of Dream Story, Viennese author Arthur Schnitzler’s 1926 novella of erotic compulsion. Dr. Bill Harford (Tom Cruise) hits the shivering streets of a dreamlike “Manhattan”—doubled for by London, with second-unit work in NYC courtesy of Arthur Jafa—after a pot-hazy domestic bust-up with wife Alice (Nicole Kidman), setting out on an odyssey to ease his bruised male ego that will lead him to what is certainly the freakiest Christmas party in all of cinema. The password at the box office is “Fidelio.”

screenings.title: Werwulf in 35mm
screenings.description: Witness Robert Eggers’ most visceral and haunting experience yet. Focus Features presents WERWULF, a harrowing tale of devotion, damnation and the devil within.

screenings.title: Fantasia
screenings.director: James Algar, Samuel Armstrong, Ford Beebe Jr.
screenings.description: The Philadelphia Orchestra, following the hand of conductor Leopold Stokowski, performs selections from Bach, Tchaikovsky, Stravinsky, Beethoven, and other giants, each accompanied by animated vignettes—most famously the mischievous Mickey Mouse vehicle “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”—to create a prodigious spectacle of music, color, and visual wit. The work of over 1,000 artists and technicians, teeming with individuated characters and pictorial invention, its “Fantasound” recording process a forerunner of surround sound to come, so undeniable was Disney’s coup de cinema as a feat of imagination and engineering that Yasujirō Ozu, who saw a seized print while working as a government censor in Singapore during World War II, would reportedly proclaim: “Watching Fantasia made me suspect we were going to lose the war.”

screenings.title: Black Narcissus
screenings.description: A group of missionary nuns led by young Mother Superior Deborah Kerr set up a convent school in the Himalayas—in fact, whipped up at Pinewood Studios in England—but soon find themselves vulnerable to the howling winds… and other temptations. Ravishingly photographed by master cinematographer Jack Cardiff, Black Narcissus builds to near psychedelic delirium in a climax involving Kathleen Byron’s Sister Ruth, driven to the edge by unfulfilled desire for dashing station agent David Farrar, whose sloshed bellowing of “The First Noel” at a Christmas service while wearing the biggest fur coat you’ve ever seen appears a potent vision of spirited seasonal cheer.

screenings.title: The Tree of Life
screenings.description: The presence of dinosaurs in The Tree of Life may be unexpected—for most of its runtime, after all, the movie is about a disgruntled, sour-faced middle-aged architect (Sean Penn) and his memories of his 1950s boyhood, spent under the eye of a cultivated-yet-tyrannical father played by Brad Pitt—but part of the peculiar brilliance of Malick’s film is, after having seen it, you can’t imagine it not containing dinosaurs. The origins of the Earth, the birth of clemency, backyard football set to the strains of Bedřich Smetana, downtown Houston as Purgatory, a constant sense of the cosmic behind the smallest gesture… Magisterial filmmaking from a Promethean talent.

screenings.title: The Train
screenings.description: Inspired by the real-life exploits of the Allied forces who worked to keep priceless artworks out of the grips of the Wehrmacht during World War II, Frankenheimer’s tough-as-nails thriller stars Burt Lancaster as a member of the French Resistance who plots to liberate a trove of masterpieces from Paris’s Jeu de Paume Museum from a cargo train also carrying Paul Scofield’s Colonel Franz von Waldheim. Praised by no less a personage than The New Yorker’s in-house railroad buff E.M. Frimbo as “the only railroad picture I’ve ever seen that wasn’t spoiled with silly technical errors.”

screenings.title: Ikiru
screenings.description: One of Kurosawa’s very greatest achievements, Ikiru shows the director at his most compassionate, affirming life through an explora­tion of death. Takashi Shimura brings a sublime pathos to his portrayal of an aging Tokyo bureaucrat who, after being diagnosed with stomach cancer, is compelled to find meaning in his final remaining days. Presented in a radically conceived two-part structure and shot with a perceptive, humanistic clarity of vision, Ikiru is a rich, multifaceted look at what it means to truly have lived.

screenings.title: Thief
screenings.description: Working with a deceptively simple premise—safecracker James Caan wants to settle down, but first he needs one last big score—Mann’s theatrical feature debut revolutionized the American action movie, fusing a detail-oriented documentary impulse, evident in its how-to heist scenes and casting of real-life cops and cons (Dennis Farina and John Santucci, respectively), with a lavish, pop-operatic style, with Mann turning the city of Chicago into a mythic, rain-slicked version of itself and a massive, immersive score courtesy Tangerine Dream. Disarmingly tender in its famed coffee shop monologue, scorched-earth savage when it turns to vengeance, Thief is a dab-handed genre piece that packs the heft of true tragedy.

screenings.title: The Grandmaster [Extended Hong Kong Cut]
screenings.description: Wong’s seventh film with Tony Leung Chiu-Wai appeared in the midst of a spate of movies about its subject, the legendary martial artist Ip Man, but being a Wong movie The Grandmaster was a thing unto itself, a travelogue through the tumultuous history of China and Hong Kong from the years of the Sino-Japanese War on, pulsing with a feeling of loss and the beauty of tradition. The set pieces rank with Wong’s very highest accomplishments, most notably a train platform showdown showpiece between Leung and Zhang, whose exquisite work playing Ip Man’s doomed rival in martial arts/forbidden love interest won her Best Actress honors at Taiwan’s 50th Golden Horse Awards.

screenings.title: Carol [DCP]
screenings.description: A Metrograph holiday tradition, back by popular demand. It starts at Frankenberg’s department store, and an exchange of glances between Carol and the girl behind the counter (Cate Blanchett and Rooney Mara, both sublime), a look that tangles up fantasies of commercial acquisition and desire. What follows is maybe the finest romance this century has yet produced, an agonizingly slow seduction where the act of shopping for and decorating a Christmas tree becomes an intensely erotic act, and delayed consummation is packed with all the anticipation that a child has for finally unwrapping a present.

screenings.title: Boogie Nights
screenings.description: The movie that irrefutably marked Anderson as a major talent, a filmmaker of élan, humor and heart, Boogie Nights follows horse-cocked picaro hero Dirk Diggler (Mark Wahlberg) into the burgeoning 1970s adult film industry, following Dirk and the business from celluloid to videotape, and from youthful optimism to adult disillusion. At the center of the chaos, tracked by a restless moving camera, is patriarchal porn maven Jack Horner, played by Burt Reynolds in Grand Old Man form.

screenings.title: Millennium Mambo
screenings.description: A stylish and seductive submersion into the techno-scored neon nightlife of Taipei, Hou’s much-misunderstood marvel stars Shu Qi (The Assassin) as an aimless bar hostess drifting away from her blowhard boyfriend and towards Jack Kao’s suave, sensitive gangster. Structured as a flashback to the then-present from the then-future of 2011, it’s a transfixing trance-out of a movie, drenched in club lights, ecstatic endorphin-rush exhilaration, and a nagging undercurrent of ennui. Hou and longtime cinematographer Lee here break from their familiar pattern of elegantly composed long shot long takes to create something both more intimate and hectic, a film whose shallow-focus images, jittery camerawork, and cramped locations evoke both the claustrophobic character of Taiwan’s capital city and, in Lee’s words, “the feeling of youth.”

screenings.title: My Neighbor Totoro
screenings.description: Two young sisters move to the country with their father and discover that the surrounding forests are home to a race of big, adorably plush beings called Totoros, who take them on a trip on a furry Cheshire Cat-like Catbus. A delight from beginning to end, and an international success that made Miyazaki a household name. Preparing the film, the director wrote: “My Neighbor Totoro aims to be a happy and heartwarming film, a film that lets the audience go home with pleasant, glad feelings. Lovers will feel each other to be more precious, parents will fondly recall their childhoods, and children will start exploring the thickets behind shrines and climbing trees to try to find a Totoro. This is the kind of film I want to make.” He did it, all right.

screenings.title: The Land Before Time
screenings.description: Fleeing natural disaster and the menacing jaws of the terrible Tyrannosaurus Sharptooth, baby Apatosaurus Littlefoot leads a party of diverse little dinos in search of their surviving family members and eventual safety in the Great Valley. A hit for producer Steven Spielberg and animator Bluth, the biggest domestic rival to Walt Disney in the feature game since the days of the Fleischer Bros., it’s ripe to be discovered by a new generation of young viewers.

screenings.title: The Hudsucker Proxy
screenings.description: “Arriving in the city, Norville Barnes, of the Muncy School of Business and Administration, has big plans. He steps into Hudsucker Industries just as Warren Hudsucker steps out, and gets his job. But will Pulitzer Prize Award-winning reporter Amy Archer find out what’s really going on? An often overlooked Coen brothers’ film with signature snappy dialogue and fantastic performances by Paul Newman, Tim Robbins, Jennifer Jason Leigh, and Charles Durning. The perfect movie over the holidays and New Year. I'll stake my Pulitzer on it!”—DeWitt Davis

screenings.title: A Tale of the Wind
screenings.description: Almost 60 years after the completion of his first film, Netherlands-born Ivens arrived in China, where he’d first traveled in 1938—here the Gobi Desert, the Dazu Rock Carvings, the Terracotta Army, and the Leshan Giant Buddha all receive visits—to produce this elliptical, ruminative last will and testament comprised of “dreams, dramatized myths and real life” [The New York Times], effortlessly reconciling cinema’s documentary and fantasy traditions. The story of a life spent, in Ivens’s words, trying to “tame the wind and harness the sea,” and a strikingly calm goodbye from a filmmaker who spent so much time focusing on the seemingly ceaseless upheavals of the 20th century.

screenings.title: Saraband
screenings.description: Thirty years after Scenes from a Marriage, Bergman revisits Marianne and Johan (Liv Ullman and Erland Josephson), the central characters of his lauded miniseries, here reunited in late life after a long separation—he recently widowed, she estranged from her adult daughters, both struggling still with unhappinesses that are seen to be largely of their own making. An exquisitely performed film at once admirably restrained and blisteringly emotional, in which Bergman and his famous creations are found facing the void with anything but mellow, self-satisfied resignation. “Powerfully, painfully honest… A meditation on the pathology of selfish relationships.” —Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

screenings.title: A Tale of Winter
screenings.description: This second film in its director’s “Tales of the Four Seasons” cycle draws inspiration from Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale while boasting of a grace and plainspoken beauty, and a reconciliation of philosophy and feeling that belong to Rohmer alone. Raising a daughter conceived during a brief but unforgettable fling, hairdresser Félicie (Charlotte Véry)—come Christmas season some five years after that fateful encounter—is found vacillating between two suitors while really loving neither, keeping a candle quietly burning for the father of her child and holding out hope that the New Year will bring her a miracle. “A nearly perfect work, in performance as well as execution.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, The Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Under The Skin
screenings.description: Glazer’s stark, moody sci-fi chiller finds mysterious, buxom Scarlett Johansson stalking the streets and highways of Scotland by night in search of lonely men to take home with her—“home” being a pitch dark, otherworldly chamber where they’re enveloped by tar pit-trap floors by their seductress, an alien in human form. A bold combination of neorealist grit—Glazer makes use of concealed cameras and nonprofessional actors—and fantastic subject matter, resulting in one of the most unique and disquieting genre films of recent years. “Visually stunning and deeply disturbing: very freaky, very scary and very erotic.”—The Guardian

screenings.title: Climax
screenings.description: A Mephistophelean musical wig-out, Noé’s immersive, rave-’til-dawn descent into a yawning open pit of mass hysteria is purportedly based on a 1990s news item about a Parisian dance troupe who collectively lost their minds on a cocktail of hallucinogens—a hypnotic, hallucinatory, and ultimately hair-raising depiction of a party that descends into delirium and violence over the course of one wintry night. “The best movie of the year gives new meaning to the term ‘bad trip.’ Frenzied dance numbers combined with LSD, mental breakdowns, and childhood trauma turn this nutcase drama into The Red Shoes meets Hallucination Generation. Freak out, baby, freak out!” —John Waters, Artforum

screenings.title: Phantom Thread [35mm]
screenings.description: One of the key scenes in Anderson’s evocation of the world of haute couture in postwar England takes place at a riotously colorful New Year’s Eve ball, but the film itself qualifies for inclusion in a holiday series by virtue of having the quality of a gift opening, with each scene unveiling new sensorial sartorial pleasures. A battle of wills between dressmaker Reynolds Woodcock (Daniel Day-Lewis), his sister, Cyril (Lesley Manville), and his muse, Alma (Vicky Krieps), Anderson’s movie has already taken on the burnished glow of a classic.

screenings.title: Sorcerer
screenings.description: This is hardcore: Brooklyn crook Roy Scheider splits town and winds up in the sweaty armpit of backwater South America, taking on a suicide mission to transport volatile nitroglycerine across a rugged, pitiless jungle in two dilapidated big rigs with fellow hard-up hard cases Bruno Cremer, Francisco Rabal, and Amidou. Suffused with otherworldly visuals and a mind-blowing score by Tangerine Dream, their first for a US studio film—Friedkin had seen them playing a gig at a decommissioned church in the Black Forest and was an immediate convert—Sorcerer “remakes” Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Wages of Fear like Led Zeppelin “remade” acoustic 1920s blues: heavy. Not for the faint of heart.
